hld:url-shortener.prompt: A shortener sees 200M new URLs per month with a 100:1 read-to-write ratio. Using 2.5M seconds per month, roughly how many redirects per second does it serve on average?
hld:url-shortener.explanation: 200M / 2.5M s = 80 writes/s, and 100:1 reads gives about 8,000 redirects/s. 800 forgets the ratio factor of 100 (it would be the write rate times 10); 16,000 doubles the figure for a peak nobody asked about.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: A service stores 2B new URLs per year for 5 years at about 500 B per record, with every record kept on 3 replicas. How much storage does it need in total?
options: 5 TB
50 TB
10 TB
15 TB
hld:url-shortener.explanation: 2B x 5 years = 10B records x 500 B = 5 TB of unique data, and 3 replicas triple it to 15 TB. 5 TB ignores replication; 50 TB is an order-of-magnitude slip (500 B is 0.5 KB, not 5 KB).

hld:url-shortener.prompt: The service expects 6 billion URLs over 5 years. Given 62^5 is about 0.92 billion and 62^6 is about 56.8 billion, what is the shortest Base62 code length with enough distinct codes (ignoring collision handling)?
hld:url-shortener.explanation: Five characters give under 1B codes, which is too few. Six give about 56.8B, which is enough on paper. Real designs often pick 7 (about 3.5T codes) so random or hashed codes rarely collide at only a tiny fraction of the space.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: A team derives each code from the first 7 Base62 characters of MD5(longUrl). Which problem must the design handle?
options: The same long URL gets a different code on every call, so duplicates pile up
Codes come out in increasing order, so anyone can walk the whole space
Two different URLs can map to the same truncated code, so inserts need a collision check and retry
MD5 output cannot be written in Base62, so codes need a different alphabet
hld:url-shortener.explanation: Truncating a hash to 7 characters keeps only about 42 bits, so distinct URLs eventually collide and the write must detect that. The hash is deterministic (same URL, same code), and it is pseudo-random, not sequential.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: Marketing wants accurate per-link click counts. An engineer proposes answering every redirect with 301 to cut server load. What is the consequence?
options: Browsers can cache the 301 and skip the shortener on repeat visits, so those clicks go uncounted
Clicks are counted twice, once by the browser and once by the server
301 forces every request to carry a new code, which breaks the cache
301 cannot carry a Location header, so redirects fail in some clients
hld:url-shortener.explanation: A 301 is a permanent redirect that browsers may cache, so repeat clicks never reach the service and analytics undercount. A 302 keeps every click visible at the cost of more traffic. Both carry Location and neither double-counts.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: Select all real drawbacks of generating codes from one global counter encoded in Base62.
options: Two requests can receive the same code when the counter is correct
The counter is a single point of failure and a write hotspot
Codes are predictable, so people can enumerate them
Codes grow too long to fit in a URL after a few thousand links
hld:url-shortener.explanation: A sequential counter is guessable and every write must pass through one place, so it limits throughput and availability. An atomic counter never hands out the same value twice, and Base62 keeps even huge counts short (7 characters reach trillions).

hld:url-shortener.prompt: One link goes viral and hits the redirect path at tens of times its normal rate. Which response fits the design best?
options: Rate-limit that code so the store is not overwhelmed
Split that key's row across more partitions so reads spread out
Serve it from the cache or a CDN edge, since the mapping never changes
Regenerate a longer code so fewer collisions occur
hld:url-shortener.explanation: A mapping is immutable, so cached copies stay correct and a hot code is served from memory or the edge. A single key lives on one partition and its replicas, so adding partitions does not help; rate-limiting punishes legitimate users; code length is unrelated.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: Incrementing a click counter row in the main URL store inside the redirect request is a good way to keep redirect p99 under 50 ms.
options: True
False
hld:url-shortener.explanation: It puts a synchronous write on the hottest path. The design emits a click event asynchronously (for example to Kafka), returns the redirect at once, and aggregates later in a stream job.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: Supporting custom aliases safely requires an atomic insert-if-absent on the code, because two users may claim the same alias at the same moment.
options: True
False
hld:url-shortener.explanation: A check-then-write sequence races: both callers see the alias as free. A conditional write (or unique constraint) on the code makes exactly one succeed and the other get a conflict response.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: Which part of a URL shortener genuinely needs strong consistency, and which can lag?
options: Both need strong consistency because they share one store
Neither, because redirects tolerate two URLs behind one code
Click counts must be strong, while code uniqueness can be eventual
Code uniqueness on create must be strong, while click counts can be eventual
hld:url-shortener.explanation: Two long URLs must never share a code, so creation needs a strong uniqueness check. Click statistics are aggregated asynchronously and a slightly stale dashboard harms nobody. Duplicate codes would send users to the wrong site.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: Which designs give collision-free codes across many API nodes without a single hot counter? Select all that apply.
options: Snowflake-style IDs (timestamp, machine id, sequence) encoded in Base62
Each node leases a block of IDs from a key-generation service and encodes them in Base62
Each node counts up from 0 on its own and encodes the value in Base62
Each node picks 7 random Base62 characters and inserts without checking for existing codes
hld:url-shortener.explanation: Leased ranges and machine-scoped Snowflake IDs are unique by construction. Independent per-node counters all start at 0 and clash immediately, and unchecked random codes will eventually collide.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: A Dynamo-style store has N=5 replicas per key. Which read/write setting guarantees that every read quorum overlaps the latest acknowledged write quorum?
hld:key-value-store.explanation: The overlap guarantee needs R + W > N. 3 + 3 = 6 > 5 works. W=2,R=3 and W=4,R=1 both sum to exactly 5, so a read set can miss the write set entirely; W=2,R=2 sums to 4.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: A store holds 20 TB of data with replication factor 3, and each node can hold 400 GB. What is the minimum node count, ignoring headroom?
hld:key-value-store.explanation: 20 TB x 3 = 60 TB raw; 60 TB / 400 GB = 150 nodes. 50 forgets replication. 200 would add roughly a third of headroom, which the question excluded.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: The cluster takes 150k client writes per second at RF=3, spread evenly over 120 nodes, and every write is applied on all 3 replicas. About how many replica writes does each node handle per second?
hld:key-value-store.explanation: 150k x 3 = 450k replica writes/s across the cluster; 450k / 120 = 3,750 per node. 1,250 ignores replication; 450,000 is the cluster total, not a per-node figure.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: A cluster of 10 equal nodes places keys with hash(key) mod 10, and an 11th node is added. Roughly what fraction of keys change owner under mod-N versus consistent hashing?
options: About 91% under mod-N, about 9% under consistent hashing
About 91% under both schemes
About 50% under mod-N, about 9% under consistent hashing
About 9% under both schemes
hld:key-value-store.explanation: With mod 10 versus mod 11 only about 1 key in 11 keeps its owner, so around 91% move. Consistent hashing hands the new node roughly 1/11 of the ring, so about 9% of keys move.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: With N=3, W=2 and R=2, two of a key's replicas are down. A sloppy quorum acks the write from one real replica plus a stand-in node outside the replica set. Why does R + W > N no longer guarantee that a later read sees the write?
options: R + W > N only holds when R is larger than W
Hinted writes are discarded once the acknowledgement is sent
The stand-in is not one of the key's replicas, so a read quorum can miss it until the hint is replayed
Coordinators read from stand-in nodes first and return stale data
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Overlap reasoning assumes both quorums are drawn from the same N replicas. A stand-in holding a hint sits outside that set, so reads can hit real replicas that lack the write until handoff completes. Hints are kept, not discarded.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: What can a vector clock tell you about two versions of a value that a wall-clock timestamp cannot?
options: Whether one version causally descends from the other or the two are concurrent
Which version is newer according to the writers' clocks
Which version the application should keep when merging
How many replicas have acknowledged each version
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Vector clocks capture causality: if neither clock dominates the other, the writes were concurrent and become siblings. They detect conflicts but do not resolve them; resolution is last-write-wins or an app-level merge.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: How does a node in a Dynamo/Cassandra-style cluster typically learn that another node is dead?
options: Nodes exchange state with random peers via gossip and suspect a peer whose heartbeat stops advancing
A central master pings every node and publishes a live list
Clients report failed requests to a registry that evicts the node at once
Each node holds a distributed lock whose expiry marks it as dead
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Gossip spreads membership and suspicion peer to peer, so there is no single master to fail. A central pinger or registry reintroduces a single point of failure, and client-reported evictions would flap on transient errors.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: An LSM-tree storage engine makes writes cheap. What is the main cost it pays in return?
options: Every write rewrites a B-tree page in place before the ack
Data in the memtable is lost on a crash because the commit log is optional
Reads may consult the memtable and several SSTables, and background compaction uses disk and CPU
Keys can live in only one SSTable, so range scans are impossible
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Writes append to a commit log and memtable and flush as immutable SSTables, so a read may probe several files and compaction must merge them later. The commit log makes crashes recoverable and range scans work fine.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: With N=3, a write acknowledged at consistency ONE followed by a read at consistency ONE can still return the older value.
options: True
False
hld:key-value-store.explanation: With R=1 and W=1, R + W = 2 which is not greater than N=3, so the read replica may not be the one that took the write. Higher levels such as QUORUM trade latency for overlap.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: Last-write-wins can silently discard one of two concurrent writes that were both acknowledged to their clients.
options: True
False
hld:key-value-store.explanation: LWW keeps the version with the higher timestamp and drops the other, even though neither write saw the other. That is why merge-friendly data such as a cart union needs vector clocks plus an application merge.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: Which mechanisms help bring a stale replica back in sync? Select all that apply.
options: Merkle-tree anti-entropy between replicas
Replaying hinted handoff writes once the owner returns
Gossip of membership state
Read repair on a read that sees mismatched replicas
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Read repair, Merkle-tree comparison and hint replay all move missing data to a lagging replica. Gossip only spreads who is alive and who owns which tokens; it carries no key-value data.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: Which are real benefits of giving each physical node many virtual nodes on the ring? Select all that apply.
options: Bigger machines can take more tokens than smaller ones
A failed node's load is shared among many peers
R + W > N is no longer needed for consistency
Load spreads more evenly across nodes
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Many small ranges smooth out hot spots, let capacity-weighted token counts, and spread both failure load and rebalancing across many neighbours. Virtual nodes affect placement only; quorum overlap is still needed.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A gateway fleet keeps limiter state for 5M active clients at roughly 120 B each in Redis. About how much memory is that?
options: 6 GB
600 MB
60 MB
12 GB
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: 5M x 120 B = 600 MB, comfortably one Redis instance. 60 MB drops a zero; 6 GB adds one. Memory is rarely the limit here; operations per second and latency matter more.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A fixed-window limiter allows 100 requests per minute. A client sends 100 requests at 12:00:59 and another 100 at 12:01:00. How many requests are admitted in those two seconds?
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: Each burst lands in a different window, so both are admitted: 200 requests in about 2 seconds, twice the intended rate. Sliding-window log and counter approaches exist to close this edge gap.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A token bucket has capacity 20 and refills 5 tokens per second, starting full. A client sends 50 requests at t=0 and another 50 at t=2s (ignore refill within an instant). How many requests are admitted in total?
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: At t=0 the full bucket admits 20. By t=2s it has refilled 2 x 5 = 10 tokens, so 10 of the second 50 pass: 30 total. Capacity bounds the burst and the refill rate bounds the long-run average.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: Two gateways both read a counter of 99 against a limit of 100, both allow the request, and both write 100. What is the right fix?
options: Read the counter first and write it back with a short TTL
Take a local in-process lock in each gateway before the read and write
Add a Redis replica and read the count from the replica
Do the check and decrement as one atomic step in Redis, such as a Lua script or INCR
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: The race is across processes, so the read-modify-write must be atomic where the state lives. A per-gateway lock cannot see other gateways, a replica read adds staleness, and a short TTL does not make read-then-write atomic.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: The limiter's Redis store becomes unreachable. Which default policy fits a public product-search API versus a login/OTP verification endpoint?
options: Both fail closed so nothing goes unprotected
Both fail open so users are never blocked
Search fails open and login fails closed
Search fails closed and login fails open
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: Search should keep serving (availability beats a short loss of throttling), whereas allowing unlimited login or OTP attempts invites brute force. A single global policy gets one of the two wrong.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A limiter allows 1,000 requests per minute per key across 1M busy keys. Which statement about a sliding-window log versus a sliding-window counter is correct?
options: The log is exact but stores up to 1,000 timestamps per key, while the counter keeps two bucket counts and approximates
The log uses less memory because a timestamp is smaller than a counter
Both are exact and differ only in speed
The counter is exact and the log approximates because timestamps are rounded
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: The log keeps one entry per admitted request, so memory grows with the limit. The counter weights the previous and current window counts, giving small constant memory and a small approximation error.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: To avoid a network hop on a very hot path, gateways keep local token buckets that sync with Redis periodically. What is the accepted cost?
options: Tokens are never refilled because Redis is only read
Rules can no longer change without redeploying gateways
Every request still waits on a Redis round trip
A key can briefly exceed its global limit while gateways act on stale state
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: Between syncs each gateway admits traffic against its own view, so total admission can overshoot a little. Teams accept this approximation in exchange for removing the network hop from the request path.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A request is rejected by the limiter. Select everything a well-behaved response should include.
options: Information about remaining quota, such as a remaining-requests header
A Retry-After value telling the client when to try again
Status 429 Too Many Requests
A 500 status so clients retry immediately
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: 429 is the standard signal, and Retry-After plus quota headers let clients back off instead of hammering. A 500 mislabels a deliberate policy decision as a server fault and invites instant retries.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: Which statements about a token bucket (capacity b, refill rate r) are true? Select all that apply.
options: Over a long period the average rate is bounded by r
A full bucket permits a burst of up to b requests
Per-client state can be just a token count and a last-refill time
It must store a timestamp for every request to be correct
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: The bucket stores a count and the last refill instant and computes refills lazily on each call. Storing every timestamp is the sliding-window log, a different algorithm.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: Requirements: 100 requests/min per API key, 1,000 requests/min per IP, and 5 logins/min per IP. How should the limiter evaluate a login request?
options: Merge all rules into one counter keyed by IP and use the smallest limit
Apply only the first matching rule and ignore the others
Check each applicable rule against its own counter keyed by (rule, client) and reject if any denies
Sum the limits and enforce the total across all clients
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: Each dimension has its own limit and identity, so each gets its own key and a request must pass all of them. One merged counter cannot express different limits and windows, and skipping rules leaves gaps.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A leaky bucket lets a client burst up to the bucket capacity and then throttles to the refill rate, while a token bucket forces output to a constant rate.
options: True
False
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: The two are swapped. A token bucket permits bursts up to its capacity; a leaky bucket drains at a fixed rate and smooths output.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: If a limiter keys only on client IP, many users behind one corporate NAT share a single quota.
options: True
False
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: They all appear as one address, so one noisy user can exhaust the allowance for everyone. Keying on API key or user id, possibly with an IP rule as a backstop, avoids that.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: A Snowflake variant gives the timestamp 40 bits of milliseconds instead of 41. About how long until the timestamp field overflows?
options: 139 years
35 years
69 years
17 years
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: 2^41 ms is about 69 years, so 2^40 ms is half of that, about 35 years. Each bit doubles or halves the lifetime, which is why the epoch is custom and recent.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: A variant uses 8 sequence bits per millisecond with the other fields unchanged. What is the maximum number of IDs one worker can issue per second?
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: 2^8 = 256 IDs per millisecond x 1,000 ms = 256,000 per second. The original 12-bit layout gives 4,096 per millisecond. 256 forgets the millisecond-to-second factor.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: A worker last issued an ID at timestamp 1000 ms and now sees its clock stepped back to 990 ms by NTP. What should it do?
options: Reset the sequence to 0 and continue with 990 ms
Continue with 990 ms, since the sequence keeps IDs distinct
Wait or refuse until the clock passes the last issued timestamp
Add the clock offset into the machine id bits
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: IDs for 990 ms may already have been issued by this same worker, so reusing that timestamp can reproduce an earlier timestamp, worker and sequence combination. Waiting or failing fast preserves uniqueness.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Why is plain UUIDv4 a poor primary key for a large B-tree indexed table?
options: It cannot be generated across data centres
Its values are random and 128-bit, so inserts scatter across index pages and the index grows larger
It needs a ZooKeeper lease before each use
It collides often at 10k IDs per second
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: Random keys land anywhere in the index, hurting locality, causing page splits and cache misses, and 128 bits cost more space than 64. Collisions are astronomically unlikely and no coordination is needed.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: A worker receives 5,000 ID requests inside one millisecond with a 12-bit sequence. What happens if it simply lets the sequence wrap to 0 and keeps the same timestamp?
options: IDs stay unique but lose time ordering
The worker id bits increment automatically to compensate
Nothing, because the sequence is unsigned and wraps safely
It issues duplicate IDs, because timestamp, worker and sequence repeat
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: Only 4,096 sequence values exist per millisecond, so wrapping reproduces earlier values within the same millisecond. The generator should spin until the next millisecond instead.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: How should the 10-bit worker ids of a Snowflake fleet be assigned safely?
options: Take the last byte of the host's IP address
Pick a random 10-bit number at startup
Use the process id modulo 1,024
Lease them from a coordination service like ZooKeeper or etcd and reclaim them when leases expire
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: Two live workers sharing an id can issue identical IDs, so assignment must be unique. Random picks collide quickly by the birthday effect, and IP bytes or pids repeat across subnets and hosts.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Flickr-style ticket servers use two databases handing out odd and even IDs. What does that solve, and what does it still lack?
options: It removes the one-database failure point, but IDs still cost a round trip and are not time-sorted
It removes the network call per ID, and it keeps IDs strictly time-ordered
It hides creation volume from outsiders, but the two servers can issue clashing IDs
It makes IDs unguessable to outsiders, but it halves the throughput of one server
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: Two servers with different parity avoid collisions and survive one failing, but each ID still needs a round trip and ordering is only roughly interleaved. IDs also still reveal volume.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Which are properties of Snowflake-style IDs? Select all that apply.
options: A worker can issue them without a network call per ID
They fit in a signed 64-bit integer
They reveal nothing about creation time
They are strictly increasing across all workers
They sort roughly by creation time
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: The layout is 64 bits with a timestamp prefix and each worker generates locally. Ordering across workers is only approximate because clocks differ, and the timestamp bits plainly leak creation time.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Compared with UUIDv4, which statements about UUIDv7 and ULID are true? Select all that apply.
options: They fit in a 64-bit integer column
They are still 128-bit values
Nodes can generate them without coordinating
A time prefix makes new inserts cluster near the end of an index
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: The time-ordered prefix improves B-tree locality, and no coordination is required like UUIDv4. They remain 128 bits, so a 64-bit column does not hold them; that is Snowflake's niche.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Snowflake IDs from two different workers are guaranteed to be strictly ordered by their real creation time.
options: True
False
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: Each worker stamps IDs using its own clock, and clocks differ by skew. IDs are roughly time-ordered, but two IDs created close together on different workers can sort the wrong way.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Using a database auto-increment ID as a public identifier can leak business volume, such as how many orders were created.
options: True
False
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: Sequential values let an observer compare two IDs over time and compute the rate of creation. Snowflake IDs also leak creation time, so this trade-off applies to time-prefixed schemes as well.

hld:notification-system.prompt: A campaign must push to 50M users within 20 minutes. What sustained send rate is required?
options: About 2.5 million per second
About 42,000 per second
About 420,000 per second
About 4,200 per second
hld:notification-system.explanation: 20 minutes = 1,200 s; 50M / 1,200 is about 41,700 per second. That is far above the 200 per second average, which is why bursts are buffered in queues and workers scale out.

hld:notification-system.prompt: A campaign burst arrives at 50k messages per second for 60 seconds, while workers can send 10k per second. How large is the queue backlog at the end of the burst?
options: 2.4 million
3 million
hld:notification-system.explanation: The queue grows by (50k - 10k) = 40k per second for 60 s = 2.4 million. 3 million forgets that workers drain during the burst; 600,000 counts only what was drained. The backlog then drains at 10k per second.

hld:notification-system.prompt: Push, SMS and email share one queue and one worker pool. The SMS provider goes down and each SMS attempt hangs. What goes wrong?
options: Messages are acknowledged and lost without retry
Stuck SMS attempts and retries occupy workers, delaying push and email too
Push and email messages are rerouted to SMS
Nothing, because retries are asynchronous
hld:notification-system.explanation: With shared capacity, a slow or failing provider consumes workers and grows a common backlog. A queue per channel isolates the failure and lets each pool scale independently.

hld:notification-system.prompt: 1,000 workers all retry a failed provider call after exactly 2s, then 4s, then 8s, and the provider keeps struggling. What is missing from the retry policy?
options: A longer first delay of 10 minutes
Jitter, so retries from different workers do not hit in synchronized waves
Retrying on a different channel for every attempt
A fixed retry interval instead of exponential backoff
hld:notification-system.explanation: Backoff alone keeps clients in lockstep, so each wave lands together and prolongs the outage. Random jitter spreads retries out. A DLQ after N attempts then bounds the work.

hld:notification-system.prompt: A worker sends a push, then crashes before acknowledging its queue message, so the queue redelivers it. How do you prevent a visible duplicate?
options: Acknowledge before sending so it can never be redelivered
Use a queue advertised as exactly-once
Disable retries after a crash
Have the next worker check the delivery log for the idempotency key before sending
hld:notification-system.explanation: At-least-once delivery means redelivery happens, so the sender must dedup using an idempotency key and a log. Acking first becomes at-most-once and loses messages when a crash comes after the ack. A small send-then-record window remains.

hld:notification-system.prompt: A bug in an upstream service loops and calls the API 500 times in a minute for the same user, each call with a different idempotency key. Which control limits the damage?
options: The idempotency key check
A per-user frequency cap before enqueueing
A dead-letter queue
Retry with exponential backoff
hld:notification-system.explanation: Distinct keys look like distinct requests, so dedup passes them all. A per-user frequency cap stops excessive volume regardless of caller bugs. Backoff and a DLQ handle delivery failures, not excess demand.

hld:notification-system.prompt: How should a 50M-user campaign be sent?
options: A loop in the API server thread that calls the provider for each user
A campaign job reads the segment in pages and enqueues per-user messages at a controlled rate into the channel queues
One synchronous API call that carries all 50M user ids
Fan out all 50M messages instantly so workers autoscale to absorb them
hld:notification-system.explanation: Paging through the segment and enqueueing at a controlled rate keeps memory bounded, lets queues buffer, and respects provider limits. A single giant request or inline loop fails or ties up the API, and an instant flood can overwhelm queues and providers.

hld:notification-system.prompt: APNs is down for an hour. What is the sensible behaviour for queued iOS push messages?
options: Move them to the SMS queue so users still get a message
Reroute them through FCM, which bypasses APNs
Drop them, since push is best-effort
Keep them in the push queue, retry with backoff and jitter, and expire stale ones by TTL
hld:notification-system.explanation: APNs is the delivery gateway to iOS, and FCM reaches iOS through APNs anyway, so rerouting does not help. Waiting with backoff and a TTL works, and SMS and email queues keep flowing independently. Dropping loses important messages.

hld:notification-system.prompt: Choosing a message broker with exactly-once semantics is enough to guarantee a user's device receives a notification exactly once, end to end.
options: True
False
hld:notification-system.explanation: Exactly-once inside the broker does not cover the provider call or the device. A crash after the provider accepts but before the ack leads to a retry, so systems use at-least-once plus idempotent dedup.

hld:notification-system.prompt: Quiet hours should be evaluated in the user's time zone, not the server's.
options: True
False
hld:notification-system.explanation: A user's 10 pm to 7 am window is local to them. Evaluating in server time would wake users abroad. Store the time zone with the preference and compare against it.

hld:notification-system.prompt: After N failed delivery attempts a notification is parked. Select all practices that apply.
options: Move it to a dead-letter queue
Keep it so it can be inspected and replayed after a fix
Drop it silently to protect queue health
Alert when the DLQ depth grows
hld:notification-system.explanation: A DLQ keeps poison or unlucky messages from blocking retries while preserving them. Alerting on its depth surfaces provider or payload problems, and silent drops lose messages.

hld:notification-system.prompt: Which signals best show that the SMS pipeline is falling behind? Select all that apply.
options: Error rate from the SMS provider
Growth of the SMS dead-letter queue
Average template length
Age of the oldest message in the SMS queue
hld:notification-system.explanation: Queue age, provider errors and DLQ growth all directly reflect delivery trouble. Template length is a static content property and says nothing about throughput or health.

hld:news-feed.prompt: A news feed uses pure fan-out on write: every new post id is pushed into each follower's cached timeline. An account with 100 million followers posts once. What is the core problem, and what is the usual remedy?
options: Post ids are no longer unique at that scale; move to UUIDs generated per follower
Reads become O(n) in the number of followees; switch the whole system to pull on read
One post triggers about 100 million cache inserts; keep pushing for normal users but merge that account's recent posts in at read time
The follow graph cannot be read for an account that large; cap followers at a fixed limit
hld:news-feed.explanation: Push makes write cost proportional to follower count, so a celebrity post becomes a huge burst of inserts. The hybrid keeps cheap O(1) reads for ordinary authors and pulls only the few celebrity authors a user follows at read time. Switching everything to pull would make every read slow to fix a problem that only a few accounts cause.

hld:news-feed.prompt: A feed service has 300M daily active users, each loading the timeline 5 times a day. Spread evenly over 86,400 seconds, roughly how many timeline reads per second is that on average?
options: About 17k per second
About 1.7k per second
About 1.7M per second
About 170k per second
hld:news-feed.explanation: 300M x 5 = 1.5 billion reads per day. Divided by roughly 86,400 seconds, that is about 17,400 reads per second on average. Peak traffic is a multiple of this, which is why the case budgets about 50k per second for peak. The other options are off by a factor of ten in one direction or the other.

hld:news-feed.prompt: Posts arrive at 50 million per day, which is about 580 per second. Under fan-out on write, the average author has 400 followers instead of 200. Roughly how many timeline-cache inserts per second does that imply?
options: About 58k per second
About 231k per second
About 460k per second
About 116k per second
hld:news-feed.explanation: 580 posts/s x 400 followers is about 231k inserts per second. The 116k option is the figure for 200 followers, so it ignores the change, and doubling write amplification doubles inserts. This is the write amplification trade-off: reads stay O(1) but write load scales with the follower count.

hld:news-feed.prompt: The timeline cache stores only post ids (a capped Redis list per user) and hydrates bodies from a post cache. Which benefits does this give? Select all that apply.
options: The timeline service no longer needs any read from the post cache or posts DB
Each cached entry is small, so many more timelines fit in memory
A deleted or edited post is reflected at hydration time without rewriting every follower's list
Capping list length bounds the memory used per user
hld:news-feed.explanation: Ids are tiny, and bodies live in one place, so edits and deletes show up at hydration and the cap bounds per-user memory. The id-only design does not remove the post lookup: that hydration step is exactly where the bodies come from, so claiming no post reads are needed is wrong.

hld:news-feed.prompt: In a hybrid feed design, a user sees a celebrity's new post because the fan-out workers insert it into that user's cached timeline just like any other post.
options: True
False
hld:news-feed.explanation: False. The point of the hybrid is that celebrity posts are not fanned out; the timeline service fetches those authors' recent posts at read time and merges them with the pre-built cache. Fanning them out would reintroduce the 100M-insert burst the hybrid exists to avoid.

hld:news-feed.prompt: A ranked feed is paged with ?page=2&limit=20, and the service re-scores and re-sorts candidates on every request. Users report seeing the same post on consecutive pages. What is the best fix?
options: Re-run ranking and drop any post the user has ever seen from the whole history
Use OFFSET pagination but sort by author id to make results deterministic
Return a cursor tied to a stable snapshot of the ranked candidate ids, and continue from it
Give each page a larger limit so users rarely reach page two
hld:news-feed.explanation: With re-ranking, scores and new posts shift positions between requests, so an offset lands on items already shown. A cursor into a fixed ranked candidate list (or one that carries the last position plus an exclusion of ids already served) keeps pages consistent. Sorting by author id would destroy the ranking.

hld:news-feed.prompt: Many accounts are inactive: they have not opened the app in weeks. Which policy best balances freshness against cost?
options: Keep fanning out to every follower's timeline so it is always fresh
Move their timelines to the posts DB and read them synchronously on every load
Delete inactive users' follow edges so fan-out has fewer targets
Skip fan-out for long-inactive users and rebuild their timeline on demand when they return
hld:news-feed.explanation: Pushing into timelines nobody reads wastes writes and cache memory. Rebuilding on demand at next login trades a slower first load for a large saving. Deleting follow edges loses user data, and the DB-only variant just moves cost to every read.

hld:news-feed.prompt: A fan-out worker consumes 'new post' events and must find all followers of the author. The follows table is only indexed by follower_id. What is the problem?
options: Followers of an author cannot be looked up efficiently, so the data also needs an index or copy keyed by followee_id
Followers must be stored inside the post row instead
A relational database cannot store a many-to-many relationship
The table needs a unique constraint on follower_id to be queryable
hld:news-feed.explanation: Fan-out asks 'who follows X', while timeline reads ask 'whom does Y follow'. Both directions are needed, which is why the data model stores the relation both ways. An index keyed only by follower_id would force a full scan for every post.

hld:news-feed.prompt: A user deletes a post that already sits in many followers' cached timelines (id lists). Which approaches are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Block the delete request until the id is removed from every follower's list
Mark the post deleted in the post store and drop ids whose post is missing or deleted when hydrating
Publish a delete event so workers remove the id from cached timelines asynchronously
Rely only on timeline TTL expiry, accepting that the post may stay visible for days
hld:news-feed.explanation: Hydration filtering gives immediate correctness, and an async delete event cleans up the lists eventually. Blocking the author on millions of list edits does not scale and is unnecessary. Relying on TTL alone leaves a deleted post visible to followers, which is a correctness and privacy failure.

hld:news-feed.prompt: Fan-out on read keeps write cost low because posting only stores one row, but timeline latency grows with the number of accounts a user follows.
options: True
False
hld:news-feed.explanation: True. Pull builds the timeline by merging recent posts from every followee at request time, so read cost scales with followee count and is hard to keep under a 200 ms target for heavy followers. That is the mirror image of push, whose reads are O(1) but writes explode.

hld:chat.prompt: A chat service has 100M daily users sending 40 messages a day each at about 100 bytes per message (400 GB/day). Roughly how much raw message data accumulates per year, before replication?
options: About 1.46 PB
About 146 TB
About 14.6 TB
About 14.6 PB
hld:chat.explanation: 400 GB/day x 365 is roughly 146,000 GB, or about 146 TB. With replication (commonly 3x) and multiple years, history reaches the petabyte scale, which is why the case partitions by chat in a wide-column store. The other options are off by factors of ten.

hld:chat.prompt: Each WebSocket gateway can hold about 500k connections. At a future peak of 250 million concurrent connections, what is the minimum number of gateways, ignoring headroom?
hld:chat.explanation: 250M / 500k = 500 gateways. In practice you add headroom for failures and spikes, so the real fleet is larger. The 250 option divides by 1M instead, and 50 and 2,500 are order-of-magnitude slips.

hld:chat.prompt: Why does the design assign a sequence number per chat rather than one global total order across all messages?
options: A global order would reveal the number of users on the platform
Global ordering is impossible because clocks differ between phones
Per-chat numbers use fewer bits, which is what allows partitioning in Cassandra
Users only need messages ordered within a conversation, and a global sequencer would be a bottleneck and single point of failure
hld:chat.explanation: Ordering only matters inside one chat, so each chat can be sequenced independently and spread across shards. A single global counter would limit throughput and availability. Clock differences matter for timestamps, but a server-assigned sequence does not depend on client clocks anyway.

hld:chat.prompt: A sender's phone sends a message, the server persists it, but the ack is lost on a flaky network. The client retries the same send. How should the server behave?
options: Store it again with a new sequence number, since the retry is a new request
Reject the retry with an error so the client gives up
Compare timestamps and keep the earlier copy only if it is under a second old
Recognise the clientMsgId as already stored and return the original msgId and seq
hld:chat.explanation: The client-generated clientMsgId makes the send idempotent: the server looks it up and returns the earlier result, so there is no duplicate and the sender learns the seq. Assigning a new seq would show the message twice. Timestamp matching is fragile and unnecessary.

hld:chat.prompt: A WS gateway crashes while handling messages. Which practices help guarantee that no accepted message is lost? Select all that apply.
options: Rely on the push notification provider to guarantee delivery
Keep messages only in gateway memory until the recipient acknowledges them
Persist the message and assign its seq before acknowledging the sender
On reconnect the client fetches any messages after its last seen seq
The client retries unacknowledged sends with the same clientMsgId
hld:chat.explanation: Durable write before ack plus idempotent client retries plus gap-fetch on reconnect cover the failure windows. Gateway memory is lost with the crash, and push providers are best effort and carry little data, so neither can be the source of truth.

hld:chat.prompt: A phone was offline for a week. What is the most sensible way for it to catch up?
options: The client sends its last seen seq per chat and pages through newer messages from the messages store
Push notifications replay each missed message to the device
The server queues every WebSocket push for a week and replays them on connect
The client re-downloads its entire history for every chat
hld:chat.explanation: Because messages are durable and ordered by seq per chat, sync is a pull: ask for everything after last-seen seq, page by page. Server-side replay buffers would be huge and push notifications are lossy. Re-downloading all history wastes bandwidth.

hld:chat.prompt: Messages are stored with chat_id as the partition key and seq as the clustering key. If the table were instead partitioned by sender_id, what would be the main consequence for loading a chat?
options: Messages would become unordered within each partition
Group chats would no longer be possible
Nothing, as long as an index on seq exists
A chat's messages would be scattered across many partitions, so reading history becomes a multi-partition scatter-gather
hld:chat.explanation: The access pattern is 'give me the recent messages of this chat'. Partitioning by chat and clustering by seq makes that one sequential read; partitioning by sender spreads it across every participant's partitions and forces merging. Order within a partition is still sorted by its clustering key.

hld:chat.prompt: At hundreds of millions of connections, long polling is generally the better choice than WebSockets because it holds less state per connected client.
options: True
False
hld:chat.explanation: False. Long polling creates repeated HTTP request/response cycles with headers and re-connection overhead for every message window, which costs more at scale. WebSockets keep one lightweight persistent connection per client, giving lower latency and less per-message overhead.

hld:chat.prompt: Presence uses a heartbeat roughly every 30 seconds that refreshes a TTL key. Why not simply mark a user offline when their connection closes?
options: Crashes, dead batteries and network loss often close nothing cleanly, so only expiry of the TTL reveals the user is gone
WebSockets cannot report disconnects at all
Presence must be eventually consistent, so explicit events are forbidden
Closing a connection is too slow to detect
hld:chat.explanation: Clean disconnect events are not guaranteed: a phone that loses signal never says goodbye. A TTL key expires on its own when heartbeats stop, so stale 'online' states self-heal. Explicit close events can still be used as an optimisation.

hld:chat.prompt: The service stores messages on the server so it can sync devices. If the product moved to end-to-end encryption, which server-side features would be limited? Select all that apply.
options: Showing message text in push notification previews generated by the server
Assigning a per-chat sequence number to each message
Server-side full-text search over message bodies
Routing a message to the recipient's gateway through the connection registry
Storing an encrypted blob so an offline device can fetch it later
hld:chat.explanation: Search and body-based previews need plaintext on the server. Sequencing, routing and storing opaque ciphertext need only metadata, so they keep working, which is why E2E chat can still do ordering and offline sync.

hld:chat.prompt: The registry says the recipient is on gateway 7, but gateway 7 has just crashed. The message was already persisted. What should happen?
options: Broadcast the message to every gateway in case the user has moved
Treat the forward failure like an offline recipient: send a push notification and let the client sync from the store on reconnect
Delete the message and tell the sender the send failed
Retry forwarding until gateway 7 is back so ordering is preserved
hld:chat.explanation: Since the message is durable, delivery is just an optimisation over the sync path. A failed forward degrades to the offline case, and the client picks it up by seq on reconnect. Blocking on a dead gateway stalls the chat and broadcasting wastes capacity.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: 500 hours of video are uploaded every minute, and one hour takes about 1.5 GB across all renditions. About how much new storage is that per day?
options: About 1.08 EB
About 108 TB
About 1.08 PB
About 10.8 PB
hld:video-streaming.explanation: 500 x 60 x 24 = 720,000 hours per day. 720,000 x 1.5 GB = 1,080,000 GB, which is about 1.08 PB. This matches the case's estimate of roughly 1 PB per day and explains why object storage is required.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: The platform serves 1 billion views per day. Spread evenly, about how many view events per second is that, and what does it suggest for counting?
options: About 1.2k/s, so a single DB row per video is fine
About 11.6k/s, and viral videos concentrate it onto few keys, so batch and aggregate asynchronously
About 1.2M/s, so a streaming job cannot keep up
About 116k/s, so views must be sharded across a hundred nodes
hld:video-streaming.explanation: 1B / 86,400 is about 11.6k per second on average, and a viral video concentrates a large share on one counter. Client-side batching plus an async aggregation job avoids a hot row and keeps the DB off the hot path. The other figures are off by 10x or more.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: Why is the uploaded video split into chunks before transcoding?
options: Chunks transcode in parallel across workers, so processing time stops scaling with video length and a failed chunk can be retried alone
CDNs cannot cache files larger than one chunk
HLS and DASH refuse to play unchunked files
Chunking reduces the final file size of each rendition
hld:video-streaming.explanation: Parallel chunk transcoding shortens time to publish to minutes and limits the blast radius of a failed worker. Segment packaging is a separate step for streaming. Chunking itself does not shrink output or relate to CDN size limits.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: A team increases segment length from 2 s to 10 s. Which outcome is most likely?
options: No change, since segment length only affects the manifest
Faster bitrate switching but higher CDN egress
Lower start-up time and fewer rebuffers on mobile
Better compression and fewer requests, but slower reaction to bandwidth changes
hld:video-streaming.explanation: Longer segments amortise keyframes and request overhead, improving efficiency, but the player can only change rendition at a segment boundary, so it reacts more slowly to drops. Short segments are the opposite trade-off.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: Which signals does an adaptive-bitrate player typically use to choose the next segment's rendition? Select all that apply.
options: A per-segment decision returned by the playback API
The video's total view count
Current buffer occupancy
Measured download throughput of recent segments
hld:video-streaming.explanation: With HLS and DASH the decision is made in the client from measured throughput and buffer level, picking from the ladder in the manifest. The server does not decide per segment, and popularity of a title is not a network signal.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: A major series launches tomorrow at 09:00 and will be watched by millions immediately. Which CDN strategy fits best?
options: Cache only the manifest and fetch segments from object storage
Pre-position the segments to edge or ISP caches beforehand during off-peak hours
Serve it from the origin and scale the origin horizontally
Pull-through caching only, since the CDN fills itself on first request
hld:video-streaming.explanation: For predictable hot content, pre-positioning moves bytes during quiet hours so launch traffic never hits the origin. Pull-through suits the long tail, but a cold start for millions would stampede the origin.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: Every view does UPDATE videos SET view_count = view_count + 1 against one row. What goes wrong for a viral video?
options: Row lock contention on a hot key serialises the writes and slows or times out the DB
Reads of that video stop working
The counter can never exceed a 32-bit value
The CDN cache is invalidated on every update
hld:video-streaming.explanation: Thousands of increments per second on one row queue behind each other on its lock. Client-side batching and an asynchronous aggregation job turn those into occasional bulk updates. Overflow is a separate matter and the CDN is not involved.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: Because egress dominates cost, maximising the CDN cache hit ratio is more important than saving transcoding compute.
options: True
False
hld:video-streaming.explanation: True. Bytes delivered to viewers dwarf the one-off cost of encoding, so each point of CDN offload cuts the dominant bill and also improves start-up latency. That is why ISP-embedded caches are worth the effort.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: Uploads use a pre-signed multipart URL to object storage instead of POSTing the file to the API servers. What is the main advantage?
options: The video is automatically transcoded by object storage
It guarantees the file is a valid video
The large upload bypasses the application tier and can be resumed part by part
It removes the need to authenticate the uploader
hld:video-streaming.explanation: The client streams bytes straight to storage, so API servers are not bandwidth bottlenecks and a failed part can be retried alone. The URL is issued after authentication, and validation and transcoding still happen later in the pipeline.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: A transcode worker crashes halfway through chunk 37 of 120. Which statements hold in a well-designed pipeline? Select all that apply.
options: The chunk's task returns to the queue and another worker retries it
The manifest is published only after all required chunks and renditions are done
Outputs are keyed by video, chunk and rendition so a re-run overwrites safely
The raw upload is deleted immediately to avoid duplicates
The whole video is re-transcoded from chunk 1
hld:video-streaming.explanation: Queues give at-least-once retries, so tasks must be idempotent. Publishing the manifest last avoids exposing a partial video. Restarting everything wastes work, and deleting the raw file would destroy the input needed for the retry.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: In this design the player fetches segments from the CDN, while the playback API only returns the manifest and metadata.
options: True
False
hld:video-streaming.explanation: True. The playback API reads video metadata and issues the manifest, and every segment request goes to the CDN edge. Proxying bytes through the API would remove the offload that makes the economics work.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: 5M drivers each send a location update every 4 s, which is 1.25M writes/s. If the interval were cut to 2 s, how many updates per second would the location service need to ingest?
options: About 1.25M per second
About 625k per second
About 2.5M per second
About 10M per second
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: 5M / 2 s = 2.5M updates per second: halving the interval doubles the rate. This is why the location path is in-memory and sharded by region rather than backed by a durable database.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: At peak the system sees about 100k ride requests per minute, and 1.25M location updates per second. About how many times larger is the location rate than the request rate?
options: About the same
About 750 times
About 75 times
About 7,500 times
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: 100k per minute is about 1,667 per second. 1.25M / 1,667 is about 750. Location ingest dominates traffic by orders of magnitude, so it gets its own in-memory design while the lower-rate, high-value trip writes go to a strongly consistent DB.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: A shard of the in-memory location index restarts and loses its contents. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: Trips in progress lose their assigned driver
Driver positions repopulate within seconds as drivers send their next updates
Matching for that region is impossible until a database backup is restored
Trip state is unaffected because it lives in the trips DB
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Locations are ephemeral and refreshed every few seconds, so the index heals itself. Trip assignments and states are persisted separately in the consistent store. That split is why in-memory speed is acceptable for locations but not for trips.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: A rider stands near the edge of an H3 cell. If matching only searches that one cell, what is the risk?
options: It will always find the geometrically nearest driver
Drivers just across the boundary in a neighbouring cell are missed, so search the cell plus its k-ring neighbours
The query will return duplicate drivers
H3 cannot index a point on an edge
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Cell boundaries are arbitrary relative to the rider, so close drivers can sit in an adjacent cell. Searching the rider's cell plus its neighbours covers the radius, and candidates are then ranked by ETA.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: Two candidate drivers: one is 300 m away across a river with the nearest bridge 8 km off; another is 1.2 km away on the same road. How should the matcher rank them?
options: By the order their location updates arrived
By estimated time of arrival along the road network
By straight-line distance, since it is the cheapest to compute
By driver rating alone
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Pickup time is what the rider experiences, so rank by ETA using road routing rather than as-the-crow-flies distance. The straight-line shortlist is a fine first filter, but not the final ordering.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: Two ride services try to claim the same driver at once. Which implementation prevents double-booking?
options: A conditional update that atomically sets state to reserved only if it is currently available
Read the driver state, check it is available, then write reserved in a separate call
Use a per-instance in-memory lock inside each ride service
Offer the driver to both riders and let the driver pick one
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Compare-and-set in the store that owns the driver state is atomic, so exactly one claim wins. The read-then-write has a race, and per-instance locks do not coordinate across multiple instances.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: Matching each rider greedily to the nearest free driver at request time always minimises total pickup time across all riders.
options: True
False
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: False. Greedy choices can steal a driver that would be a much better fit for the next rider, leaving a poor global result. Batching requests over a short window and solving an assignment problem can lower total wait, at the cost of a little added latency.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: A driver is reserved for an offer, then closes the app and never responds. If reserved had no expiry, what would happen?
options: The location index would delete the driver
The rider would be charged
Nothing, because reserved automatically reverts
The driver would stay unavailable and the rider would never be offered another driver
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: A reservation without a timeout becomes a stuck lock: the driver is invisible to matching and the rider waits. Offers have a short timeout after which the driver returns to available and the next candidate is tried.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: A rider cancels at the same instant the driver accepts. What is the safest way for the trips DB to resolve it?
options: Queue both and process them in a random order
Accept the cancel always because it is cheaper
Use a state-conditional update so only one transition from the current state succeeds, and report the loser's failure
Apply both and let the later timestamp win
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Trip transitions should be compare-and-set on the current state (or a version), so concurrent events cannot both apply. The loser gets a clear failure and the trip stays in a valid state. Timestamp-wins is vulnerable to clock skew.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: Which statements compare geohash and H3 correctly? Select all that apply.
options: Geohash cells have identical area at every latitude
H3 removes the need to search neighbouring cells
Neighbouring geohash cells can have very different prefixes, so a prefix match can miss nearby points
All six neighbours of an H3 hexagon have centres at the same distance
Geohash prefix length can be shortened to search a coarser area
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Hexagons give uniform neighbour distances, geohash prefixes give simple hierarchical lookups but suffer boundary cases. Both need neighbour searches near edges, and geohash cells narrow towards the poles so their area is not constant.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: Dropping an occasional driver location update over UDP is acceptable because the next update, a few seconds later, supersedes it.
options: True
False
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: True. Location pings are ephemeral and only the latest one matters, so loss is tolerable and cheaper than reliable delivery. The same logic would be wrong for trip state changes, which must never be lost.

hld:payment-system.prompt: 1M payments a day are processed (about 12 per second). Each payment posts 4 ledger entries. About how many ledger entry rows per second is that on average?
options: About 460
About 4,600
About 46
About 4.6
hld:payment-system.explanation: 1M x 4 = 4M rows per day, divided by 86,400 seconds gives roughly 46 per second. That is easily handled by one SQL primary with replicas, which is why the hard part is correctness rather than throughput.

hld:payment-system.prompt: A client sends POST /v1/payments and the connection times out with no response. What should it do?
options: Retry with a fresh Idempotency-Key to avoid a conflict
Show a failure and ask the customer to try again
Retry with the same Idempotency-Key so the service returns the original result or finishes the same payment
Look up the order and create a payment only if none exists
hld:payment-system.explanation: The key lets the server tell a retry from a new payment: it returns the stored outcome rather than charging twice. A new key would risk a second charge, and telling the customer to retry manually invites double payment.

hld:payment-system.prompt: A request arrives with an Idempotency-Key that was used earlier, but the amount in the body differs. What should the service do?
options: Reject it as a key reuse with a different request, since the stored request hash does not match
Process it as a new payment with the new amount
Return the first response silently, ignoring the new amount
Overwrite the stored request and charge the difference
hld:payment-system.explanation: A matching key with a different request fingerprint indicates a client bug. Silently returning the old result hides it and process-as-new can double charge. Rejecting with an error is the safe, explicit behaviour.

hld:payment-system.prompt: Which statements about a double-entry ledger are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Keeping the account's balance as a single mutable column is enough for audit
A refund should edit the original entry in place to keep the table small
The entries of one transaction may be committed in separate DB transactions
Each transaction's debits and credits must balance, so its entries sum to zero
Balances are derived from entries, and corrections are new reversing entries
hld:payment-system.explanation: Balanced entries make errors detectable, and append-only entries with reversals preserve history. In-place edits and single mutable balances destroy the audit trail, and splitting a transaction's entries across commits can leave the books unbalanced after a crash.

hld:payment-system.prompt: The provider's webhook for a charge arrives before your API call to the provider returns. What design handles this correctly?
options: Delay processing webhooks by a fixed 30 seconds
Always trust the API response over the webhook
Make state transitions idempotent and forward-only, so whichever of the webhook or API response arrives first is applied and the second is a no-op
Reject the webhook until the API response has been stored
hld:payment-system.explanation: The payment state machine accepts either source, matches on provider_ref, and ignores stale or duplicate events, so ordering does not matter. Dropping the webhook risks losing the only notification, and fixed delays are guesswork.

hld:payment-system.prompt: The service commits the payment to the database and then publishes 'payment captured' to Kafka in a separate step. What is the flaw?
options: Kafka cannot store payment data
A crash between the commit and the publish loses the event, so downstream systems never learn of the capture
Publishing is too slow after a commit
The database transaction will not roll back
hld:payment-system.explanation: This is a dual write: two systems cannot be updated atomically. With a transactional outbox, the event is written in the same DB transaction and a relay publishes it, so the event exists if and only if the commit does.

hld:payment-system.prompt: Every ledger transaction sums to zero, yet the daily provider settlement file totals 1 rupee more than your records. Where do you look first?
options: Inside the ledger, to find the entry that does not balance
Re-run the day's webhooks
Check the database indexes
Match payments with the settlement file by provider reference and compare amount and status for each one
hld:payment-system.explanation: The ledger's internal consistency is already guaranteed, so the gap is between your records and the provider's. Reconciliation line by line on provider_ref finds missing, extra or differing items. Replaying webhooks may add duplicates.

hld:payment-system.prompt: It is safe to skip verifying a webhook's signature if the endpoint URL is long and kept secret.
options: True
False
hld:payment-system.explanation: False. URLs leak through logs and proxies, and anyone who learns it could forge 'payment captured' events. The signature proves the provider sent the payload, so it must be verified, ideally with a timestamp check against replay.

hld:payment-system.prompt: Which storage choice best fits the ledger and payments tables, given 12 payments per second but zero tolerance for lost or doubled money?
options: A document store with last-write-wins
An in-memory cache with periodic snapshots
An eventually consistent key-value store that favours availability
A relational database with ACID transactions, accepting reduced availability in a partition
hld:payment-system.explanation: The workload is small, so scale is no issue; what matters is atomic multi-row ledger writes and UNIQUE constraints for idempotency. An SQL database provides both. Eventual consistency and last-write-wins can lose or duplicate money.

hld:payment-system.prompt: The provider call times out after 10 s with an unknown outcome. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Retry later with the same provider idempotency key, or query the provider for status
Mark the payment pending or unknown instead of failed
Mark it failed and let the customer retry with a new key
Immediately issue a refund in case it was charged
hld:payment-system.explanation: The charge may have succeeded, so the outcome must stay unresolved until the provider confirms it via status query, webhook or a safe retry with the same key. Failing it early invites a second charge, and an immediate refund may refund money never taken.

hld:payment-system.prompt: A payment was captured for 100. Two refund requests for 60 each arrive simultaneously, and each reads 'refunded so far = 0' before writing. What can happen, and what fixes it?
options: Only the first succeeds because SQL serialises everything by default
Both succeed, refunding 120; lock the payment row or use a conditional update on the refunded total inside the transaction
Both fail, so nothing is refunded; add a retry
The ledger will reject one because it always balances
hld:payment-system.explanation: This is a classic check-then-act race: both pass the validation. A row lock (SELECT FOR UPDATE) or a conditional update such as refunded_total + 60 <= amount makes the check atomic. A balanced ledger does not prevent over-refunding, since both entries balance.

hld:payment-system.prompt: Two concurrent requests with the same Idempotency-Key are safe because the UNIQUE constraint lets only one insert succeed, so the other can wait for or return the first result.
options: True
False
hld:payment-system.explanation: True. The unique key constraint is enforced by the database even under concurrency, so one request wins the insert and the other sees a conflict and returns or waits for the stored result. A check-then-insert in application code would not give this guarantee.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: Two buyers click the same available seat at the same instant. The booking API runs an atomic conditional UPDATE (set status to held WHERE seat is still available). What happens?
options: Both UPDATEs run, the later one overwrites the earlier, and both buyers see success
Whichever request reached the load balancer first wins, as enforced by the API tier
The database raises a deadlock error to both buyers and neither of them gets the seat
Only one UPDATE changes the row; the other affects zero rows and that buyer is told the seat is taken
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: The database serialises writes to the same row, so the second UPDATE re-evaluates its WHERE clause, sees status is no longer available and changes nothing. The service reads the affected-row count to decide the winner. Arrival order at the load balancer does not decide it, and there is no deadlock because only one row is touched.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: A popular on-sale has 10 million users trying to buy and only 50,000 seats. If every user makes exactly one hold attempt, what is the maximum share of attempts that can succeed?
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: 50,000 / 10,000,000 = 0.005 = 0.5%. At least 99.5% of attempts must fail, which is why the system should absorb most of that traffic in front of the database (waiting room, CDN, fast rejects) instead of letting every request reach the inventory table.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: A virtual waiting room admits users to the booking API at 2,000 users per second. Roughly how long until the first 50,000 users (the number of seats) have been admitted?
options: About 42 minutes
About 2.5 seconds
About 4 minutes
About 25 seconds
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: 50,000 / 2,000 = 25 seconds. The admission rate is set by what the backend can handle, and queue position gives fairness. In practice more than 50,000 are admitted because some buyers abandon, but the arithmetic shows how a controlled rate turns a 10M-user spike into a manageable stream.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: A buyer's card payment succeeds, but by the time the order is confirmed their 10-minute hold has already expired and another buyer may have taken the seat. What is the correct handling?
options: Confirm anyway and flip the seat to sold, since the buyer has already paid
Flip held to sold only if the hold is still valid for this buyer; otherwise refund or void the payment
Ignore the payment event and let the buyer retry the whole purchase from scratch
Extend the expired hold silently so the paid order can proceed
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: Confirmation must be a conditional write: it succeeds only if the seat is still held by this hold and not expired. If the seat was resold, forcing it would double-sell. The payment must then be refunded or voided. Ignoring it leaves the customer charged with no ticket.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: Why does the design reserve seats with one atomic conditional write in the inventory database instead of acquiring a distributed lock per seat for the whole checkout?
options: A lease-based lock can expire while its holder is paused or delayed and still believes it owns the seat, whereas the conditional write is checked by the database that holds the truth
A lock cannot be created for a seat that is not yet in the database
Locks cannot expire, so an abandoned checkout would block the seat forever
Distributed locks are always at least ten times slower than SQL updates
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: Lease-based locks have the classic problem that the holder can stall (GC pause, network delay), the lease expires, and a stale writer proceeds. A check-and-set inside the source of truth has no such window. Locks can expire, so the third option is wrong, and the other two claims are not true in general.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: A teammate proposes this seat-hold logic. What is wrong with it under concurrent traffic?
options: Two requests can both read available before either updates, so both get OK and one hold silently overwrites the other
Each statement is atomic, so the code is safe and only slightly slower than a single UPDATE
The SELECT should use a larger isolation level only for reads, which makes the later UPDATE safe
The seat row needs a TTL column, and adding one removes the race
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: This is a check-then-act race: the check and the write are separate steps, so both requests can pass the check. The fix is to put the condition in the UPDATE itself (WHERE status = 'available') and inspect the affected-row count. Per-statement atomicity does not make the pair of statements atomic.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: A user asks to hold three adjacent seats in one request. The conditional UPDATE over those three seat ids reports only 2 rows changed. Given that the group must stay together, what should the service do?
options: Mark the two held seats as sold to avoid leaving gaps in the seat map
Roll back the two changes (or run it in one transaction) and report a conflict so the request is all-or-nothing
Retry the same UPDATE in a loop until all three rows change
Keep the two seats held and tell the user to pick a third one later
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: A multi-seat hold succeeds only if all rows changed, so a partial result must be undone. Keeping two seats locks inventory for a request that cannot complete, looping may spin forever on a seat someone else is paying for, and marking seats sold without payment is plainly wrong.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: Which of these measures protect the database at on-sale time? Select all that apply.
options: Rejecting excess requests early with a quick overload response instead of queueing them inside the API
Raising the hold time to 60 minutes so fewer hold requests are made
Having clients retry failed requests immediately and without backoff
Serving the static seat-map layout from a CDN
A waiting room that admits users at the rate the backend can handle
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: Admission control, edge caching of static content and early load shedding all keep traffic away from the inventory DB. A longer hold mostly locks seats up and does not reduce attempts much, and immediate retries without backoff multiply load during exactly the moment the system is saturated.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: Holds expire after about 10 minutes. Which approaches correctly make an expired hold's seat available again? Select all that apply.
options: Treating a held seat with an expired hold time as available inside the conditional write or the read path
Relying on the buyer's browser to call a release endpoint when the tab is closed
A background worker that periodically releases holds whose expiry time has passed
Relying on database row locks timing out, which frees the seat automatically
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: Server-side expiry, either by a sweeper or by a lazy check of hold_expires_at, is reliable. Browsers crash, lose connectivity or never fire the call, so client-driven release cannot be trusted. Row locks last for a transaction and say nothing about the application-level hold state stored in a column.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: Making the seat hold duration much longer always increases sales, because buyers get more time to finish paying.
options: True
False
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: A longer hold improves conversion for slow payers but keeps seats unavailable to others, so abandoned checkouts lock up inventory that could have sold. It is a trade-off between conversion and locked-up stock, not a free win.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: Someone argues that once the waiting room limits admissions to 2,000 users per second, the conditional UPDATE is no longer necessary. What is wrong with that argument?
options: The waiting room limits overall rate but not contention, since admitted users can still pick the same seat at the same time
At 2,000 users per second the database cannot handle any writes at all
Waiting rooms are only advisory and users can bypass them in every implementation
The conditional UPDATE is only needed for payments, not seat holds
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: Rate limiting protects capacity; it does not make two requests for the same seat mutually exclusive. Even at low volume two admitted buyers can click the same seat in the same millisecond, so correctness still comes from the atomic conditional write.

hld:collaborative-docs.prompt: Two editors place the cursor at the same position in a shared document and type different characters at the same moment. What outcome should the system guarantee?
options: Both edits are kept and every replica converges to the same text, with the server's ordering deciding which character comes first
Each user keeps seeing their own version until one of them saves
The server rejects the second edit and asks that user to retype it
The later keystroke by wall-clock time overwrites the earlier one
hld:collaborative-docs.explanation: The no-lost-edits and convergence requirements mean both characters survive and everyone ends with identical text. In OT the server orders the concurrent ops and transforms them against each other. Overwriting or rejecting loses work, and per-user diverging versions violates convergence.

hld:collaborative-docs.prompt: A product needs users to edit for hours offline on phones and merge later, with no always-on central ordering server. Which approach fits best and what is its main cost?
options: Last-writer-wins on the whole document, at the cost of occasionally dropping edits
Operational transformation, because it needs less per-character metadata
Pessimistic document locking, at the cost of only one editor at a time
A CRDT such as Yjs or Automerge, at the cost of extra per-character metadata
hld:collaborative-docs.explanation: CRDTs give each element a unique, ordered identity so replicas can merge without a central authority, which suits offline-first. The price is metadata and tombstone overhead. OT depends on a central server to order and transform ops, so it is a poorer fit for long offline work.

hld:collaborative-docs.prompt: Assume 10 editors per active document, each producing about 5 operations per second, and the server broadcasts every operation to the other editors of that document. How many operations per second does the session server receive and send for one active document?
options: Receives 50, sends 50
Receives 500, sends 450
Receives 50, sends 450
Receives 50, sends 500
hld:collaborative-docs.explanation: Incoming: 10 editors x 5 ops/s = 50 ops/s. Each op goes to the 9 other editors, so outgoing = 50 x 9 = 450 messages/s. The fan-out is why per-document traffic is dominated by sends, and why it still fits comfortably on a single server for one doc.

hld:collaborative-docs.prompt: At peak, 20,000 documents are being actively edited, each at 50 operations per second. One session server can sustain 10,000 operations per second. Ignoring headroom, what is the minimum number of session servers?
hld:collaborative-docs.explanation: Total load = 20,000 x 50 = 1,000,000 ops/s. Dividing by 10,000 ops/s per server gives 100 servers. Real deployments add headroom for failover and spikes, and routing by document id keeps each doc on one server so the load can be spread by hashing.

hld:collaborative-docs.prompt: All editors of a document are routed to one session server chosen by consistent hashing on the document id. That server crashes. What is the right recovery?
options: The document becomes read-only until an operator restores the server

The ring assigns the document to another server, which loads the latest snapshot and replays the ops after it from the log; clients resend unacknowledged ops, which are de-duplicated by clientId and sequence number
The new server starts from an empty document and clients re-send their entire local text
Clients switch to a peer-to-peer mesh because the log is no longer trusted
hld:collaborative-docs.explanation: Because ops are persisted in an append-only log with periodic snapshots, any server can rebuild the in-memory state. Clients retry unacknowledged ops and (clientId, seq) lets the server drop duplicates. Starting from empty or going read-only would lose edits or availability.

hld:collaborative-docs.prompt: A document has accumulated a million edits and opening it is slow because the server replays the whole ops log. What is the standard fix?
options: Load the most recent snapshot and replay only the operations recorded after it
Delete old operations once they are a day old to keep the log short
Sort the ops log by operation size so large ops are applied first
Store the document only in memory and rebuild it from clients on demand
hld:collaborative-docs.explanation: Periodic snapshots bound replay work to the tail of the log. Deleting ops would destroy version history and undo, memory-only state loses durability, and reordering ops by size would break the causal order that convergence depends on.
