hld:collaborative-docs.prompt: A prototype has the server assign a sequence number to each incoming op and broadcast it. Clients simply apply every received op as-is on top of their local text, even though they also applied their own pending edits immediately. Two users concurrently edit near each other. What goes wrong?
options: Presence updates will be delayed by the extra ordering
The server runs out of sequence numbers
Nothing, since the server's ordering already guarantees convergence
Op positions refer to different document states on different clients, so replicas diverge unless ops are transformed against concurrent ones
hld:collaborative-docs.explanation: An op like insert at index 5 means something different if a concurrent edit already shifted the text. Ordering alone is not enough: with OT the concurrent ops are transformed so their positions are adjusted. Without it, replicas apply the same ops to different states and drift apart.

hld:collaborative-docs.prompt: Which statements about CRDT-based editing (such as Yjs or Automerge) are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Each character or element gets a unique, ordered identifier so replicas can merge without a central ordering server
Merging is independent of the order in which updates arrive, so offline edits can be merged later
They require a central server to assign a total order to every operation
They keep extra metadata, including markers for deleted content, which makes documents larger
They cannot support offline edits
hld:collaborative-docs.explanation: CRDTs are designed so concurrent updates commute and converge without central coordination, which is what enables offline work. The trade-off is metadata, including tombstones for deletions. Requiring a central total-order server is the OT model, not the CRDT model.

hld:collaborative-docs.prompt: A document store keeps an append-only ops log per document plus periodic snapshots. Which benefits does this give? Select all that apply.
options: No need to route a document's editors to the same server
Fast document loads, since only the ops after the latest snapshot need replaying
No need to order concurrent operations, since the log orders them automatically
Version history, since any earlier version can be rebuilt by replaying ops up to that point
hld:collaborative-docs.explanation: The log plus snapshots give history, undo and bounded load time. They do not resolve concurrency by themselves: something (the session server in OT, or the CRDT merge rules) still has to order or merge concurrent ops, and server affinity is a separate design choice for keeping state in memory.

hld:collaborative-docs.prompt: Cursor positions and presence information should be appended to the durable ops log so they show up in version history.
options: True
False
hld:collaborative-docs.explanation: Presence is ephemeral and changes constantly, so it is kept in memory and broadcast, not persisted. Writing it to the log would multiply write volume and pollute history with data nobody needs to replay or undo.

hld:autocomplete.prompt: A search box has 20 million daily active users, each running 10 searches per day and typing about 5 characters per search with one request per keystroke. Using 86,400 seconds per day, what is the average request rate?
options: About 5,800 requests per second
About 1,200 requests per second
About 11,600 requests per second
About 116,000 requests per second
hld:autocomplete.explanation: 20M x 10 x 5 = 1,000,000,000 requests per day. Dividing by 86,400 gives about 11,574, or roughly 11.6k per second on average. Peak would be a multiple of that, so capacity must be planned above the average.

hld:autocomplete.prompt: Why does the design store the top-K completions at every trie node instead of finding them when the request arrives?
options: It lets the trie fit in less memory than storing only the words
It removes the need to aggregate query logs
A lookup becomes proportional to the prefix length, rather than requiring a walk of the whole subtree below the prefix
It guarantees suggestions are always perfectly fresh
hld:autocomplete.explanation: For a short prefix such as 'a', the subtree holds a huge part of the vocabulary, so ranking it per keystroke is far too slow for a 50 ms budget. Pre-computed top-K lists make the lookup O(prefix length). It costs extra memory, and does nothing for freshness or log aggregation.

hld:autocomplete.prompt: The UI shows at most 10 suggestions and no re-ranking is done at request time. An engineer sets K to 1,000 at every trie node to 'be safe'. What is the main consequence?
options: Memory use grows roughly 100x for the cached lists, while almost none of the extra entries are ever shown
Suggestion quality gets worse because the lists are noisy
Lookups slow down to O(K) per keystroke
The trie cannot be sharded any more
hld:autocomplete.explanation: Cached lists live at every node, so total memory scales with K. Going from 10 to 1,000 inflates that part about 100 times with entries that are never returned. Reading the first 10 of a sorted list is still cheap, and sharding is unaffected.

hld:autocomplete.prompt: A breaking-news query suddenly spikes, but the main trie is rebuilt only every few hours from aggregated logs. Which approach gets the new query into suggestions fast without rebuilding the trie constantly?
options: Run stream aggregation with time-decayed counts and merge the resulting small set of trending terms into results at query time, while the full trie is still rebuilt periodically
Wait for the next scheduled rebuild, since users never notice staleness
Lower K to 1 so new queries replace old ones faster
Rebuild the whole trie after every logged search
hld:autocomplete.explanation: A streaming job with decay detects trends in minutes and feeds a small overlay that the suggest service merges with the big, periodically rebuilt trie. A per-search rebuild is far too expensive, K=1 destroys quality, and waiting hours misses the 'trending' requirement.

hld:autocomplete.prompt: The trie is rebuilt offline from fresh counts. Why is the new trie swapped in atomically instead of mutating the live trie in place?
options: It guarantees every replica swaps at exactly the same instant
Readers never see a half-updated structure with inconsistent cached top-K lists, and no locking is needed on the hot read path
In-place updates are impossible in any in-memory data structure
Atomic swaps make the new trie use less memory than the old one
hld:autocomplete.explanation: Updating counts in place would require changing top-K lists along every ancestor on the path while serving reads. Building off to the side and swapping a pointer keeps reads lock-free and consistent. Replicas may swap at slightly different times, which is fine given tolerated staleness.

hld:autocomplete.prompt: To shard the trie, a team splits it into 26 shards by the first letter of the prefix. What problem will they hit?
options: Top-K lists cannot be stored on more than one machine
Prefixes beginning with different letters cannot be looked up on the same machine
Some letters get far more queries than others, so a few shards are hot and the load is uneven; ranges should be chosen using measured query load
Sharding by prefix makes it impossible to rebuild the trie
hld:autocomplete.explanation: Query traffic is heavily skewed across starting letters and prefixes, so equal-width alphabet ranges produce unbalanced shards. Splitting prefix ranges based on observed traffic or size balances them. Each request carries a full prefix, so routing to one shard is easy.

hld:autocomplete.prompt: The service must offer personalised suggestions while still hitting 20k requests per second at p99 under 50 ms. Which design is most sensible?
options: Drop personalisation entirely, since it cannot be done under 50 ms
Fetch the shared global top candidates from the trie, then blend in or re-rank using a small amount of per-user recent data in the service
Build a separate trie for every user and keep them all in memory
Compute personalised suggestions with a full database scan of that user's history on every keystroke
hld:autocomplete.explanation: A hybrid keeps the expensive, shared structure global (and cacheable) and applies cheap per-user adjustment on top. Per-user tries do not scale in memory, and a history scan per keystroke blows the latency budget. Light re-ranking is routinely done within tens of milliseconds.

hld:autocomplete.prompt: Which client-side or edge techniques cut load on the suggest service? Select all that apply.
options: Caching popular prefixes at a CDN
Bypassing the CDN for short prefixes, since they have the most distinct results
Sending a request on every keystroke and never caching, to keep results real-time
Caching responses per prefix in the browser
Debouncing keystrokes so a request is sent only after the user pauses briefly
hld:autocomplete.explanation: Debouncing and per-prefix caching both avoid repeated or wasted requests, and CDN caching serves popular prefixes without reaching the service. Short prefixes are the most popular and repeated, so they are the best candidates for caching, not the worst. Since suggestions may be minutes stale, caching is acceptable.

hld:autocomplete.prompt: The requirements say suggestions may be a few minutes stale. Which design choices does that tolerance allow? Select all that apply.
options: Taking a distributed lock on the trie for every search so all replicas stay perfectly in sync
Updating the trie synchronously before returning each search result
Aggregating query counts asynchronously from logs instead of in the request path
Caching suggest responses for a short time at the CDN or browser
Letting replicas swap to a freshly built trie at slightly different moments
hld:autocomplete.explanation: Tolerated staleness is what makes caching, asynchronous aggregation and non-simultaneous swaps acceptable. Locking per search or updating synchronously puts writes on the hot path of a read-heavy, latency-critical service, which is the opposite of what the relaxed requirement lets you avoid.

hld:autocomplete.prompt: The best way to keep popularity ranking current is to increment the matching trie nodes' counts synchronously on every search request.
options: True
False
hld:autocomplete.explanation: That puts a write fan-out (every ancestor node and its top-K list) on the hot request path of a read-heavy service. The usual approach is to log queries, aggregate counts offline or in a stream, and rebuild or overlay the trie periodically.

hld:web-crawler.prompt: A crawler must fetch 2.6 billion pages per month. Using a 30-day month (about 2.6 million seconds), what is the sustained fetch rate?
options: About 10,000 pages per second
About 100,000 pages per second
About 1,000 pages per second
About 100 pages per second
hld:web-crawler.explanation: 30 x 86,400 = 2,592,000 seconds. 2.6e9 / 2.6e6 = 1,000 pages per second on average. The case's own figure follows the same arithmetic: 1B pages per month is about 400 per second.

hld:web-crawler.prompt: A crawler fetches 3 billion pages per month and the average page is 150 KB. How much raw content does it download per month?
options: About 45 TB
About 450 TB
About 4.5 PB
About 45 PB
hld:web-crawler.explanation: 3e9 x 150e3 bytes = 4.5e14 bytes = 450 TB. The case's own estimate (1B pages x 100 KB = 100 TB) scales the same way, which is why a blob store and compression are part of the design.

hld:web-crawler.prompt: Why does the crawler map each host to one back queue served by a single worker at a time, instead of having all workers pull any URL from one shared queue?
options: A shared queue cannot hold more than a million URLs
A single queue per host makes DNS lookups unnecessary
With a shared queue many workers could request the same site at once, overloading it and violating politeness rules
Per-host queues make the fetched pages smaller
hld:web-crawler.explanation: Politeness means a bounded request rate per host. If any worker can take any URL, nothing stops dozens of them from hitting the same server simultaneously. One queue per host with one active worker and a delay between requests enforces the limit by construction.

hld:web-crawler.prompt: A Bloom filter is used to check whether a URL has already been seen before enqueueing it. The filter answers 'seen' for a particular URL. What can you conclude?
options: Nothing, since a Bloom filter can wrongly miss URLs that were previously added
The URL has not been seen, because the filter reports the opposite of what it stores
The URL has probably been seen, but with a small chance it is new and would be wrongly skipped
The URL has definitely been seen, because Bloom filters never make mistakes
hld:web-crawler.explanation: Bloom filters have false positives but no false negatives. A 'not seen' answer is certain, a 'seen' answer may be wrong. The cost is occasionally skipping a never-crawled URL, which the memory savings usually justify; a backing store can confirm when it matters.

hld:web-crawler.prompt: Two mirror sites serve the same article but each wraps it in different ads and footers. Which technique best detects that these pages are near-duplicates?
options: Compare SHA-256 hashes of the full page bytes
Compare simhash-style fingerprints and treat pages with a small Hamming distance as duplicates
Compare the URLs after normalisation
Compare the response size in bytes
hld:web-crawler.explanation: An exact content hash changes if even one byte differs, so it only finds byte-identical copies. Simhash produces similar fingerprints for similar content, so a small Hamming distance flags near-duplicates. URLs differ on mirrors and equal sizes prove nothing.

hld:web-crawler.prompt: The crawler has many machines running the URL frontier. How should URLs be partitioned across them?
options: By file extension, so similar content types are crawled together
By a hash of the host, so a site's politeness queue and delay state live on one machine
By a hash of the full URL, so each page is spread evenly
Randomly per fetch, so no machine becomes a hotspot
hld:web-crawler.explanation: Politeness needs one place that knows the last-request time and queue for each host. Hashing by host keeps all of a site's URLs together; hashing by full URL would scatter one site over many machines, each unaware of the others' requests.

hld:web-crawler.prompt: One page changes every hour and another changes about once a year. A crawler re-crawls both on a fixed 30-day interval. What is the main problem and the better approach?
options: Fixed intervals are the most efficient since they keep the schedule predictable
Neither page needs re-crawling after the first fetch
Both pages should be re-crawled every hour to be safe
The fast-changing page is stale most of the time and the slow one wastes budget; adapt the interval to each page's observed change rate
hld:web-crawler.explanation: Crawl budget is finite. A uniform interval under-serves frequently changing pages and over-serves static ones. Estimating change frequency and re-crawling accordingly improves freshness for the same budget. Crawling everything hourly would blow the budget.

hld:web-crawler.prompt: Fetch workers each resolve the host name through a blocking DNS call for every single URL, with no caching, at hundreds of fetches per second. What is the issue and the usual fix?
options: DNS must be resolved from scratch on each request because records change within seconds
DNS lookups become a throughput bottleneck; cache resolutions per host and resolve asynchronously
The fix is to crawl by IP address only and skip host names
DNS lookups are free, so the design is fine
hld:web-crawler.explanation: Synchronous resolution adds latency to every fetch and can saturate the resolver. Many URLs share a host, so caching with TTL respect removes most lookups, and asynchronous resolution avoids blocking workers. Crawling by raw IP breaks virtual hosting.

hld:web-crawler.prompt: A calendar page links to 'next month' forever, producing infinitely many distinct URLs. Which controls help the crawler escape such traps? Select all that apply.
options: Re-fetching robots.txt more often
Capping the number of pages fetched per host
Making the Bloom filter bigger
Limiting crawl depth
Limiting the maximum URL length
hld:web-crawler.explanation: Depth, URL-length and per-host budget caps bound how far a generated-link trap can drag the crawler. A bigger Bloom filter only reduces false positives, and every trap URL is genuinely new anyway. robots.txt is about permissions, not infinite link spaces.

hld:web-crawler.prompt: The URL frontier uses front queues and back queues. Which statements describe their roles correctly? Select all that apply.
options: Front queues fetch and cache robots.txt for each host
Front queues order URLs by priority, such as importance and change rate
Back queues are organised per host so that a host is fetched by one worker at a time with delays
Back queues detect near-duplicate page content with simhash
hld:web-crawler.explanation: Priority is handled in front queues and politeness in per-host back queues. Content fingerprinting happens after parsing, on the fetched pages, and robots.txt and DNS are cached by the fetch side per host. Neither belongs to the queue tiers.

hld:web-crawler.prompt: To stay polite, a crawler must download a host's robots.txt again before every single page request to that host.
options: True
False
hld:web-crawler.explanation: robots.txt is cached per host and refreshed periodically (respecting expiry). Re-fetching before every request would double the load on the site, which defeats politeness. A cached copy is the standard approach.

hld:file-sync.prompt: A service stores 1 exabyte of logical user data (500M users x 2 GB). Cross-user dedup finds that 30% of the bytes are duplicates of data already stored. How much unique data must be stored, before replication?
options: About 700 PB
About 1.3 EB
About 7 EB
About 300 PB
hld:file-sync.explanation: 1 EB = 1,000 PB. Removing 30% leaves 70% = 700 PB. Duplicates become references to an existing block instead of a new copy, which is why content-addressed storage saves so much at this scale. Replication or erasure coding for durability then multiplies this figure.

hld:file-sync.prompt: With 4 MB blocks, 1 EB of data is about 250 billion blocks (1e18 / 4e6 = 2.5e11). If the index stores a 32-byte SHA-256 hash per block, roughly how big is the hash column alone?
options: About 800 GB
About 800 TB
About 80 TB
About 8 TB
hld:file-sync.explanation: 2.5e11 x 32 bytes = 8e12 bytes = 8 TB. Add paths, revisions, locations and indexes and metadata is far larger, which is why block size trades dedup granularity against metadata overhead and the metadata layer must be sharded.

hld:file-sync.prompt: A 1 GB file (256 blocks of 4 MB) has one byte overwritten in place, without changing the file length. With block hashes checked first, how much must the client upload?
options: The whole 1 GB, because the file hash changed
About 4 MB, only the one block whose hash changed
About 256 hashes and no block data
About 1 byte, the byte-level delta
hld:file-sync.explanation: Only the block containing the modified byte has a new hash; the other 255 hashes match blocks the server already holds. The client uploads that one 4 MB block and commits a new block list. The 256 hashes are sent in the commit, but the new block still has to go up.

hld:file-sync.prompt: A laptop was offline for an hour and reconnects. How does it learn what changed in the user's folders?
options: It asks for changes after the last journal cursor it saw, then fetches the new metadata and any missing blocks
It asks the notification service to push every missed message, which are all retained forever on the connection
It compares file timestamps with the server clock
It re-downloads every file and compares them locally
hld:file-sync.explanation: The per-namespace journal gives a monotonic cursor, so a returning client can ask exactly for entries after its last position. This catches up reliably regardless of how long it was away. Full re-downloads are wasteful and clock comparisons are unreliable between devices.

hld:file-sync.prompt: Two devices edit the same file offline and each commits against base revision 5. What should the server do?
options: Reject both and ask the user to redo the edits
Accept both and silently let the second overwrite the first
Accept the first commit as revision 6, reject the second as based on an outdated revision, and keep its content as a conflicted copy
Merge the two block lists byte by byte automatically
hld:file-sync.explanation: The commit carries baseRevision so the server can detect that the file has moved on. The loser is not discarded: keeping a conflicted copy means no data is lost. Overwriting loses work, and a generic automatic byte-level merge can corrupt arbitrary file types.

hld:file-sync.prompt: A client is uploading 50 new blocks for a modified file and crashes after 30 of them. What should the metadata state be, and what happens on restart?
options: The file shows a half-written state so other devices can start downloading the first 30 blocks
The file revision already points to a block list with 20 missing blocks; the client later fills them in
The server deletes the previous version of the file as soon as the first new block arrives
Metadata is unchanged and still points to the old revision; on restart the client asks which blocks are missing, uploads the remaining 20, and then commits
hld:file-sync.explanation: Blocks are uploaded first and the commit is the single atomic step that points the path at the new block list, validated to reference only existing blocks. A crash before that leaves the old revision intact. The 30 uploaded blocks are reused on retry by their hashes, or garbage-collected if never referenced.

hld:file-sync.prompt: Why does the design keep file metadata in a strongly consistent database but blocks in cheap object storage?
options: Object storage cannot be replicated across data centres
Metadata is far larger than the data, so it needs the best hardware
Committing a new revision needs an atomic compare-and-swap on a path's revision, whereas immutable content-addressed blocks need no coordination
Blocks change constantly, while paths and revisions never change
hld:file-sync.explanation: Correctness hinges on metadata: concurrent commits to one path must be serialised with a revision check. Blocks are immutable and named by their hash, so duplicates are harmless and they can live in cheap, highly durable storage. The reverse is true of what changes: paths and revisions change, blocks do not.

hld:file-sync.prompt: 100 million online devices each poll the server every 5 seconds asking 'any changes?', and nearly every reply is empty. Roughly what request rate is that, and what is the better alternative?
options: About 20 million requests per second; the load is fine because empty responses are free
About 2 million requests per second; use full file listings instead
About 500 thousand requests per second; use polling every second instead
About 20 million requests per second; use long-poll with a cursor so the server answers only when something changes
hld:file-sync.explanation: 100,000,000 / 5 = 20,000,000 requests per second, almost all wasted. Long-polling (or push) holds the connection and replies when the journal advances, trading some open connections for far fewer requests and lower latency. Empty responses still cost connections, TLS, auth and CPU.

hld:file-sync.prompt: Which benefits come from identifying blocks by a content hash and never modifying them? Select all that apply.
options: Blocks can be cached aggressively because their content never changes
Identical blocks across files and users are stored once
The metadata database becomes unnecessary because the hash identifies the file
Uploads can be retried safely, since re-uploading the same block is idempotent
Block contents can be edited in place cheaply
hld:file-sync.explanation: Content addressing gives dedup, idempotent uploads and cache-friendliness. It does not replace metadata: paths, revisions, block lists and permissions still live in the database. Blocks are immutable, so edits create new blocks rather than modifying existing ones.

hld:file-sync.prompt: A team shrinks the block size from 4 MB to 1 MB. Which effects should they expect? Select all that apply.
options: The metadata database gets smaller
Fewer chances of finding duplicate blocks across files
A small edit re-uploads less data
Each file's block list and the total metadata grow
Transferring a file needs more block requests
hld:file-sync.explanation: Smaller blocks give finer-grained dedup and smaller re-uploads per change, at the price of more hashes, more metadata rows and more requests per file. Dedup opportunities generally increase, not decrease, and metadata clearly grows rather than shrinks.

hld:file-sync.prompt: When two devices make conflicting offline edits to the same file, automatically merging them is the safest default because it avoids creating extra files.
options: True
False
hld:file-sync.explanation: Files are often opaque binaries, so an automatic merge can corrupt data. Keeping both versions as a conflicted copy loses nothing and lets the user reconcile. Auto-merge is only appropriate for formats where the system understands the structure.

hld:ad-click-aggregator.prompt: Peak click traffic is 500,000 clicks per second and each click event is about 100 bytes. What raw ingest bandwidth must the click trackers and the Kafka tier sustain at peak, before replication?
options: About 500 MB/s
About 5 MB/s
About 50 MB/s
About 5 GB/s
hld:ad-click-aggregator.explanation: 500,000 x 100 B = 50,000,000 B/s, about 50 MB/s. The average rate (10B clicks/day is roughly 115k/s, about 11.5 MB/s) is lower, but you size for peak. Being off by 10x in either direction is the usual slip when converting events per second to bytes per second.

hld:ad-click-aggregator.prompt: Raw clicks are archived for 30 days at roughly 1 TB per day, and the archive keeps 3 copies of every object. About how much physical storage does that archive need?
options: About 300 TB
About 30 TB
About 900 TB
About 90 TB
hld:ad-click-aggregator.explanation: 30 days x 1 TB = 30 TB of logical data, and 3 copies make 90 TB physical. Forgetting the copies gives 30 TB. This cost is the price of being able to reprocess history after a bug fix, which is the raw retention versus reprocessing trade-off.

hld:ad-click-aggregator.prompt: A mobile SDK retries the click request when a response times out, so the tracker sometimes receives the same click twice. Billing must not double count. Which approach is most robust?
options: Subtract a fixed estimated duplicate percentage, measured from a sample, from every minute's total
Tell the SDK never to retry, so duplicates cannot occur, and accept that some real clicks are lost
Make the load balancer reject any second request from the same IP address within a one-second window
Attach a unique clickId in the SDK, dedupe on it in the job and write results idempotently
hld:ad-click-aggregator.explanation: A client-generated clickId makes a retry recognizably the same event, so the job can drop it within the window and idempotent writes keep replays harmless. Disabling retries loses billable clicks, IP rules also drop legitimate distinct clicks (shared NATs), and a fixed percentage is simply inaccurate for billing.

hld:ad-click-aggregator.prompt: A phone is in a tunnel and uploads clicks 8 minutes after they happened. Billing must attribute each click to the minute in which it actually occurred. Which windowing basis achieves that?
options: Processing time, meaning the clock of the stream job when it sees the record
Event time, with watermarks deciding when a window may close
Log-append time, meaning when the record was appended to the Kafka log
Arrival time, meaning when the click request reached the edge proxy
hld:ad-click-aggregator.explanation: Event time uses the timestamp carried by the click, so a late arrival still lands in its true minute; watermarks and allowed lateness decide how long to wait for stragglers. Processing, log-append and edge-arrival times all reflect when the system saw the click, which would shift the late click into a later minute.

hld:ad-click-aggregator.prompt: One viral ad gets 40% of all clicks. The Kafka topic is keyed by adId, and you double the partitions from 64 to 128, yet one partition is still overloaded. Why does this not help?
options: Every record for that ad still hashes to one partition, so one consumer gets the whole hot stream
Stream job parallelism is capped at the original partition count
New partitions stay empty until the next retention cycle, when Kafka rebalances old data into them
Kafka assigns keys to partitions round-robin, so the hot ad keeps moving between them
hld:ad-click-aggregator.explanation: Partitioning by key sends all records with the same key to the same partition however many partitions exist. The fix is to spread the key itself: salt it (adId#n) or pre-aggregate locally, then merge the partial counts downstream. Adding partitions only helps when keys are diverse.

hld:ad-click-aggregator.prompt: A bug in the minute-aggregation logic over-counted for the last 3 days. Raw clicks are archived, and the OLAP table is keyed by (ad_id, minute). What is the cleanest way to correct the numbers?
options: Delete the last 3 days of aggregates and let new incoming traffic gradually refill them
Run the aggregate rows themselves through the fixed job, since they already hold the counts
Divide the stored counts by the average over-count factor observed in a sample of the affected minutes
Replay the archived raw events through the fixed job and upsert over the bad rows
hld:ad-click-aggregator.explanation: Aggregates have already thrown away the per-click detail, so only the raw log can be reprocessed correctly. Replaying it through the corrected job and upserting by (ad_id, minute) overwrites the wrong rows idempotently, which is the Kappa-style replay or the daily batch recompute. Scaling or deleting rows cannot restore true counts.

hld:ad-click-aggregator.prompt: Dashboards need numbers within a minute or two, but invoices must be exact. Which serving policy satisfies both?
options: Use the batch path for dashboards and the streaming path for invoices
Bill from the streaming totals the instant each minute closes, because they are the freshest available
Hold dashboards back until the daily batch finishes so that they always agree with the invoices
Stream results for dashboards; bill from totals reconciled by a batch recompute once late data settles
hld:ad-click-aggregator.explanation: Freshness and accuracy pull in opposite directions, so each consumer gets what it needs: low-latency approximate streaming figures for dashboards, and reconciled figures (after late events and retries are resolved) for money. Billing from the live stream risks late-data errors; the other two options invert or delay the tools needlessly.

hld:ad-click-aggregator.prompt: Select all statements that are correct about watermarks and allowed lateness in an event-time streaming job.
options: A watermark is the engine's heuristic claim that events older than some event time are no longer expected
A watermark guarantees that no event older than its timestamp can ever arrive
Events later than the allowed lateness can go to a side output or the archive and be fixed by a batch reconciliation
Raising allowed lateness reduces memory use because windows can close sooner
Allowed lateness keeps window state around so a straggler can still revise an already emitted result, at the cost of extra state
hld:ad-click-aggregator.explanation: A watermark is a progress estimate, not a guarantee, so stragglers are possible. Allowed lateness trades memory and revised outputs for completeness, and events beyond it can be reconciled later from the raw archive. Longer lateness means windows stay open longer, so memory goes up, not down.

hld:ad-click-aggregator.prompt: A Flink job restarts from its last checkpoint and re-reads some Kafka records it had already processed. Which sink designs still avoid double counting? Select all that apply.
options: Commit consumer offsets to Kafka before processing each record
Commit sink writes through a two-phase, transactional sink coordinated with checkpoints
Add each emitted window count onto the stored counter with an increment
Insert a +1 row for every click as it is processed
Upsert each window's absolute count keyed by (ad_id, minute) so a replay overwrites the same row
hld:ad-click-aggregator.explanation: Idempotent upserts and checkpoint-coordinated transactional sinks make a replay produce the same final state. Per-click inserts and increments apply the effect again on every replay, and committing offsets before processing is at-most-once: a crash can lose clicks instead of duplicating them, which breaks billing the other way.

hld:ad-click-aggregator.prompt: In a checkpointed stream pipeline, 'exactly-once' means each click record is physically delivered over the network only one time, with no replays after failures.
options: True
False
hld:ad-click-aggregator.explanation: Records can be re-read and re-sent after a crash. What the engine provides is effectively-once state and output: checkpoints restore state, and transactional or idempotent sinks keep replayed records from changing the result twice. Treating it as no-replay delivery leads people to skip idempotent sinks.

hld:ad-click-aggregator.prompt: With tumbling one-minute windows keyed by adId, a single click event can be counted in two different windows.
options: True
False
hld:ad-click-aggregator.explanation: Tumbling windows are fixed-size and do not overlap, so each event belongs to exactly one window. Overlap is a feature of sliding windows, where an event can fall in several. Double counting in this pipeline comes from retries and replays, not from the window shape.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: A 10M-player game stores one all-player sorted set in about 1 GB of Redis memory. Product also wants a separate board for each of the last 12 months, each containing all players, plus the all-time board. Roughly how much memory do these boards need?
options: About 120 GB
About 1.3 GB
About 2 GB
About 13 GB
hld:leaderboard.explanation: Each board costs about 1 GB (roughly 100 B per member x 10M), and there are 1 + 12 = 13 boards, so about 13 GB. Memory scales with the number of boards, which is why you keep only active players in old seasons or archive them to a database.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: The score service handles 5,000 updates per second, and each update is also archived as a roughly 50-byte event in the scores database. About how much new history does that add per day?
options: About 216 GB
About 2.2 GB
About 21.6 GB
About 2.2 TB
hld:leaderboard.explanation: 5,000/s x 86,400 s is about 432 million events per day, and 432M x 50 B = 21.6 GB. The sorted set stays small because it stores one entry per player; the durable history grows with every update, which matters for retention and partitioning of the DB.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: A game server reports that player p42 earned 25 more points. Higher scores must rank first, and the API then needs p42's 0-based position from the top. Which Redis command pair does that?
options: ZADD lb 25 p42, then ZRANK lb p42
ZADD lb 25 p42, then ZREVRANK lb p42
ZINCRBY lb 25 p42, then ZREVRANK lb p42
ZINCRBY lb 25 p42, then ZRANK lb p42
hld:leaderboard.explanation: ZINCRBY adds the delta to the existing score, whereas ZADD would overwrite the total with 25. ZREVRANK counts from the highest score, while ZRANK counts from the lowest, so it would report the position from the bottom of the board.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: Two players both have a score of 5,000 in a Redis sorted set. How does Redis order them relative to each other, and what does this mean if the product rule is 'whoever reached the score first ranks higher'?
options: Randomly on each query, so the product rule cannot be implemented with sorted sets at all
By insertion order, so the product rule is already satisfied without any extra work
By the time of their last ZINCRBY, so the product rule is already satisfied without any extra work
By member string, so the product rule needs the achievement time folded into the score
hld:leaderboard.explanation: Members with equal scores are ordered lexicographically by member value, not by who got there first. To rank earlier achievers higher you encode time into the score (for example a composite of score and an inverted timestamp that still fits a double's precision) so ties disappear.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: The weekly board must reset every Monday at 00:00 for 10M players while reads continue. Which approach is best?
options: At midnight, run a cron job that removes every member of the current set one at a time
Delete the key at midnight and then re-add all 10M players to the new set with a score of zero
Put the week in the key name, switch writes to the new key at the boundary, archive the old one
Keep a reset marker on each player and filter out stale scores at read time on every query
hld:leaderboard.explanation: A key per season or week (for example lb:2026-W41) makes the reset a pointer switch: the new board starts empty and the old one is archived or expired. Removing 10M members one by one or deleting and reloading the key is slow and risks blocking Redis or showing a half-built board, and read-time filtering adds cost to every query.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: A 100M-player game wants to show 'you are in the top 3%' in near real time (scores visible within a second) without keeping an exact rank in one giant sorted set. Which approach fits?
options: Recompute every player's percentile once each night using a full sort of all scores in the database
Scan a random 1% sample of the players on every single request
Use the Redis Top-K structure to track the position of every individual player in the whole game
Keep counts per score bucket and estimate percentile from the buckets above the player
hld:leaderboard.explanation: A histogram of counts per score bucket updates in O(1) and a percentile is the sum of buckets above you divided by the total, which is accurate to bucket width. Top-K only tracks heavy hitters, not every player's position, a nightly sort misses the one-second freshness need, and per-request sampling is expensive.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: ZREVRANK for player p42 returns 1204 (0-based from the top). The page should show 5 players above p42, p42 herself, and 5 players below. Which range read returns exactly those 11 entries?
options: ZREVRANGE lb 1204 1214 WITHSCORES
ZREVRANGE lb 1194 1214 WITHSCORES
ZREVRANGE lb 1199 1204 WITHSCORES
ZREVRANGE lb 1199 1209 WITHSCORES
hld:leaderboard.explanation: Positions 1199 to 1209 inclusive are 5 above (1199-1203), p42 (1204) and 5 below (1205-1209), 11 entries. The call costs O(log N + 11) after the rank lookup, so it is cheap even at 10M members. In practice clamp the start at 0 for players near the top.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: A 100M-player board is split across 8 Redis shards by hashing the player id, each shard holding a sorted set of its own players. Select all statements that hold.
options: The global top 100 needs the top 100 from every shard, merged
A single score update must be applied on every shard to keep ranks consistent
Taking only the top 13 from each shard (100 / 8) is enough for the global top 100 because hashing balances load
A player's exact global rank needs a count of higher-scoring members from every shard, summed
hld:leaderboard.explanation: A shard can hold all of the top 100 by chance, so each shard must contribute 100 candidates before merging. Exact rank is a count of members with higher scores across all shards, a scatter-gather. An update only touches the shard that owns the player. This cost is why exact ranks get expensive at huge scale.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: Redis loses the sorted set after a failure with no usable snapshot. Select all sound ways to restore the board.
options: Bulk-load each player's total from the scores database into a fresh sorted set
Replay the season's durable score events into a new sorted set
Let new score updates gradually repopulate the set and ignore players who are inactive
Ask each game client to re-submit the score it remembers locally
hld:leaderboard.explanation: The durable store is the source of truth, so both loading totals and replaying events rebuild an exact board. Client-reported scores are untrusted and invite cheating, and letting traffic repopulate the set silently drops inactive players and produces wrong ranks for everyone below them.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: The sorted set should be treated as a rebuildable hot view, with the durable score history in a database or stream as the source of truth.
options: True
False
hld:leaderboard.explanation: Redis gives fast ranks and top-N reads, but the board must survive a lost node, a bad deploy or an audit of suspicious scores. Keeping score events in a durable store lets you rebuild the sorted set at any time, so Redis can stay purely a serving structure.

hld:leaderboard.prompt: Reading the top 100 with ZREVRANGE takes time proportional to the total number of players, so with 10M players it needs a separate precomputed cache.
options: True
False
hld:leaderboard.explanation: A skip-list-backed sorted set finds the start of the range in O(log N) and then walks the 100 entries, so the cost is O(log N + 100), nearly independent of 10M members. A precomputed copy is rarely needed for correctness, only perhaps to absorb very hot read traffic.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: At peak, 2M users are connected and each sends a location every 30 s. Each user has about 40 online, opted-in friends who must receive every update. Roughly how many pub/sub deliveries per second does the system perform?
options: About 2.7 million
About 270,000
About 67,000
About 27 million
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: 2,000,000 / 30 is about 66,700 updates/s, and 66,700 x 40 is about 2.7 million deliveries/s. The 67,000 figure is just the publish rate, forgetting fan-out. The multiplier of online friends dominates the load, which is why it is the number to cap for very high-degree users.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: About 33,000 pings per second are written as 50-byte history rows, which is roughly 142 GB per day if every ping is kept. If you store only one of every six pings (about one every 3 minutes), roughly how much history per day results?
options: About 240 GB
About 140 GB
About 24 GB
About 2.4 GB
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: 33,000 / 6 = 5,500 writes/s, x 50 B = 275 KB/s, x 86,400 s is about 23.8 GB per day, roughly a sixth of 142 GB. Sampling (or a short TTL) is how history stays affordable, and it also reduces the privacy exposure of stored trails.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: Why does the design fan out live locations through per-user Redis pub/sub channels instead of a Kafka topic per user?
options: Redis pub/sub guarantees delivery and ordering for every subscriber, which Kafka topics cannot provide
Kafka topics cannot be created or removed while the cluster is running in production
Kafka cannot push messages to WebSocket gateways
Tens of millions of topics are impractical, while ephemeral channels are cheap and a lost update is harmless
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: A channel in Redis is a lightweight in-memory subscription list with no stored history, which suits data that is replaced every 30 s. Per-user Kafka topics would mean tens of millions of partitions' worth of files and metadata. Redis pub/sub is actually at-most-once, and Kafka topics can be created dynamically.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: User A publishes a new location. In the subscription-based design, what does the location service itself do to fan the update out?
options: Reads A's friend list and loops over it, sending a message to each online friend's gateway in turn
Writes A's cache entry and publishes once to A's channel; Redis delivers to subscribed gateways
Queries a geohash index for every user near A and then sends a message to each of those users
Writes the update into every friend's inbox row and then waits for the clients to poll for it
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: Friends' gateways subscribed to A's channel when they connected, so publish is a single operation and Redis performs the fan-out. Looping over 400 friends per update, or polling inboxes, puts the work and latency on the application tier. A geohash search is unnecessary because the friend list already bounds candidates.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: Clients send a location every 30 s. An engineer sets the loc:{userId} cache TTL to 25 s so that inactive users disappear quickly. What goes wrong?
options: Redis drops all pub/sub subscribers of a user whenever that user's cached key expires
Nothing breaks; a shorter TTL only makes the friends list fresher and costs nothing extra
Active users expire between pings and flicker; the TTL should exceed about two intervals
Redis refuses TTLs shorter than a minute, so every location write fails with an error
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: With a TTL below the update interval every user's entry lapses before the next ping, and a single lost update on a flaky network also evicts them. A TTL of about 60-120 s keeps active users visible through one missed ping while still clearing inactive ones without a cleanup job.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: A gateway fleet is redeployed by restarting every node at once, and every client reconnects immediately. What is the risk, and what is the standard mitigation?
options: Location data is permanently lost across the restart, so deploys must wait for acks=all
A reconnect storm overloads the balancer; drain nodes gradually and use jittered client backoff
Friend lists go stale during the restart, so cache TTLs should be shortened to one second
Sticky routing breaks the WebSocket upgrade, so it should be disabled for the deploy
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: Millions of simultaneous reconnects each trigger auth, friend lookup and cache reads at the same instant. Draining gateways a few at a time spreads the load, and randomized (jittered) exponential backoff stops clients from retrying in lockstep. Location loss is not the issue, since the next ping repairs the state.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: Because of flaky networks, a client receives a friend update with ts=100 after it already showed the update with ts=130. What is the right handling?
options: Average the two positions together to smooth the friend's apparent movement
Apply it, because the most recently received message is always the most accurate one
Drop it, because only an update newer than the stored timestamp replaces the position
Hold everything and sort it by arrival order at the server before showing it to the user
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: Updates can be duplicated or reordered, so the timestamp decides which one wins: anything not newer than the stored value is discarded. Applying the late packet would move a friend backwards, and averaging produces a position the friend was never at. The system relies on the next ping anyway, so dropping is cheap.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: A user's phone loses signal and the app is killed, with no clean disconnect. Select all mechanisms that make the system cope.
options: The gateway unsubscribes from the friends' channels when it closes the socket
The server waits for an explicit logout message before removing the user
The location cache entry expires through its TTL, so the user drops out of friends' lists
The gateway's heartbeat timeout detects the dead socket and cleans up the connection and its subscriptions
The last known location stays visible until the user next sends an update
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: Mobile clients vanish without saying goodbye, so the server must detect it itself: heartbeats find dead sockets and closing them releases the subscriptions, while the TTL makes the user disappear without a cleanup job. Waiting for a logout, or keeping stale locations indefinitely, would leave ghosts and violate the privacy goal.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: Select all statements that are correct about geohash and quadtree indexes for finding nearby places.
options: A geohash radius query needs only the point's own cell, with no neighbours
Two nearby points can have very different geohash prefixes if they sit on opposite sides of a cell boundary
Friend lookup requires a geohash index because the candidate set is otherwise unbounded
A quadtree splits a crowded cell into four, so dense areas get finer cells than sparse ones
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: A shared geohash prefix implies closeness but not the reverse, so a radius query scans the cell plus its 8 neighbours. Quadtrees adapt cell size to density at the price of an in-memory structure to maintain. Friend lookup does not need either index, because the friend list already bounds the candidates.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: Redis pub/sub keeps no history and can miss messages for a subscriber that is briefly disconnected, which is acceptable here because the next location update arrives within about 30 seconds.
options: True
False
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: Pub/sub is at-most-once with no replay. Since each ping replaces the previous one and the cache holds the latest position, a missed message is repaired by the next update or by the cache read on reconnect. Durable delivery would add cost for data nobody needs.

hld:nearby-friends.prompt: Showing each friend an exact distance is safe because only mutual friends see it, so triangulation by a malicious friend is not a concern.
options: True
False
hld:nearby-friends.explanation: A friend can move around and read distances from several points, then intersect the circles to find the exact position. Mitigations are coarse distance buckets, rate limiting, and not exposing precise values, which is the accuracy versus leakage trade-off.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: A tile pyramid has 4^z tiles at zoom level z. You pre-generate every tile for zoom levels 0 through 10 inclusive and render deeper zooms on demand. About how many tiles are pre-generated?
options: About 350 thousand
About 1.4 million
About 1.05 million
About 4.2 million
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: Zoom 10 alone has 4^10 = 1,048,576 tiles, and levels 0-9 add about a third as many: the sum is (4^11 - 1)/3 = 1,398,101, roughly 1.4 million. Each level has 4x the previous one, which is why high zooms (zoom 21 is about 4.4 trillion) cannot be pre-rendered.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: 1M location pings per second of about 100 bytes each land in Kafka, and the topic keeps 3 hours of data. Before replication, about how much storage is that?
options: About 11 TB
About 360 GB
About 1.1 TB
About 108 GB
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: 100 B x 1M/s = 100 MB/s. Over 3 hours (10,800 s) that is 1,080,000 MB, about 1.1 TB. One hour is 360 GB, which is the tempting wrong answer. Replication would multiply this further, which is why the pings are aggregated quickly and only kept for hours.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: A map app wants rotation, smooth zoom and a dark theme without producing a separate tile set for each style. Which tile format fits, and what does it cost?
options: Raster tiles at double resolution, re-rendered on the server for each requested style
Vector tiles: the client renders them, in exchange for small payloads and easy restyling
Raster tiles, with the clients simply stretching and rotating the downloaded images
Vector tiles, but each style still needs its own pre-rendered tile set stored on the CDN
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: Vector tiles carry geometry and attributes (protobuf), so one tile set supports any style, rotation and smooth zoom, and the payload is smaller than a raster image. The cost is that the client must render. Raster tiles are baked images tied to one style, so each style or rotation means different assets.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: Dijkstra on a continental road graph explores far too many nodes for a cross-country query. What do contraction hierarchies do about it, and what is the main price?
options: They cut the graph into independent tiles and run Dijkstra on each, so routes cannot cross a tile border
They precompute shortcuts that skip minor nodes so queries climb to major roads; the price is preprocessing and live-traffic weights
They sort roads by speed limit and search only highways, ignoring local roads even near the start and the end of a trip
They cache the answer for every origin and destination pair that has ever been requested before
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: Shortcuts let a query touch only thousands of nodes instead of millions, but they are computed from edge weights, so live traffic invalidates them unless the variant can re-weight shortcuts quickly. The other options either ignore local roads, rely on a cache that cannot cover all pairs, or make cross-region routes impossible.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: The map data is updated, but tiles are served from a CDN with long cache lifetimes. How do you avoid serving stale tiles without invalidating everything?
options: Have every client append a random query string to each tile request it makes
Purge the entire CDN cache every single time the map data is updated by the data team
Set the cache lifetime to only a few seconds so that every tile refreshes constantly
Put the map version in the tile URL so new requests use new cache keys, leaving old tiles valid
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: Tiles are immutable per map version, so a versioned path (or tileset id) makes a new version a new cache key, with no purge and no cold CDN. A global purge causes a stampede on the origin, tiny lifetimes destroy the hit rate, and random query strings bypass the cache entirely.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: A driver starts a 3-hour trip right now. Which ETA computation is most sensible?
options: Use posted speed limits only, since traffic conditions cannot be predicted reliably by any system
Live speeds for nearby edges, historical weekday and time-of-day speeds for later edges
Use historical speeds for every edge of the route, ignoring live data entirely
Use live speeds on every edge of the route, because live data is always the freshest
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: The jam you see now at a segment 2 hours away may be gone by the time you reach it, so far-away edges use typical speeds for the expected arrival time, while nearby edges use live data. Live-only ignores the future, and historical-only ignores the incident right in front of the driver.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: The rerouting service finds a route that is 20 seconds faster for a driver, and traffic readings fluctuate every minute. What policy best balances ETA quality and driver experience?
options: Reroute only when the driver explicitly asks for a new route in the app
Push a new route only when the saving beats a meaningful threshold, avoiding flip-flopping
Never reroute during a trip, because ETAs are only estimates and not guarantees to the driver
Push every faster route to the driver immediately, because the ETA should always be minimized
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: Constantly switching between near-equal routes distracts drivers, confuses them and loads the servers with recomputations and pushes. A threshold, often with hysteresis, keeps reroutes for significant slowdowns where the saving justifies the interruption.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: The road graph is partitioned into geographic regions, each held in memory on one routing node. Select all statements that hold.
options: A closed bridge forces every region's graph to be rebuilt
Every routing node must keep the entire global graph in memory
Within a region the router can compute an exact route using only that node's memory
Cross-region trips use precomputed boundary-node distances and stitch the regional segments together
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: Regions are sized to fit on one node, so intra-region routing is exact and local, and cross-region routes are stitched via boundary nodes. A map change rebuilds only the affected partition and its boundary shortcuts, and the new version is swapped in atomically, so global rebuilds and full-graph nodes are not needed.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: Navigation clients stream location data so the system can learn traffic. Select all sound design choices for this pipeline.
options: Pings are snapped to road edges and aggregated into average speeds per edge per few-minute window
Raw pings are kept briefly in Kafka, and only aggregates are retained long term
Devices upload batched pings to save battery and radio use
Each ping is written synchronously into the road graph's adjacency lists
Every user's full GPS history is stored indefinitely to improve ETAs
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: Batching cuts battery and bandwidth, map matching plus windowed aggregation turns noisy points into an edge-speed signal, and short retention limits both storage and privacy exposure. Indefinite per-user history is unnecessary and risky, and the routing graph is a read-optimized structure that is not mutated per ping.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: A* search with a heuristic that never overestimates the remaining travel time (such as straight-line distance at maximum speed) still returns an optimal route, while exploring fewer nodes than Dijkstra.
options: True
False
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: An admissible heuristic keeps A* optimal because it never discards a path that could be cheaper, and the heuristic steers the search toward the goal so fewer nodes are expanded. It is still too slow at global scale, which is why production systems add preprocessing such as contraction hierarchies.

hld:maps-navigation.prompt: A map pyramid has 2^z tiles in total at zoom level z.
options: True
False
hld:maps-navigation.explanation: Each zoom level has 2^z columns and 2^z rows, so 4^z tiles in total. Each level quadruples the tile count, which is why the case keeps pre-generating only low zooms and renders high zooms lazily.

hld:message-queue.prompt: A topic ingests 600 MB/s. One partition sustains about 30 MB/s on your brokers. Each consumer in the group can process at most 10 MB/s, and a partition is read by only one consumer in a group. What is the minimum partition count that satisfies both limits?
hld:message-queue.explanation: Write throughput needs at least 600 / 30 = 20 partitions. Consumption needs 600 / 10 = 60 consumers, and since each partition goes to a single consumer in the group you need at least 60 partitions. The larger requirement wins, and teams usually add headroom on top.

hld:message-queue.prompt: Ingest is 500 MB/s and the topic uses replication factor 3. Followers fetch each byte from the leader. About how much additional replication traffic crosses the broker network per second?
options: About 250 MB/s
About 500 MB/s
About 1.5 GB/s
About 1 GB/s
hld:message-queue.explanation: Each byte is copied to 2 followers, so replication traffic is 2 x 500 MB/s = 1 GB/s. The 1.5 GB/s figure is total inbound traffic if you also count the producers' own writes. It is easy to forget that the network cost scales with replication factor minus one.

hld:message-queue.prompt: You must tolerate the loss of any single broker without losing an acknowledged message, while still accepting writes during that failure. Which settings do that?
options: Replication factor 3, acks=all, min.insync.replicas=3
Replication factor 3, acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2
Replication factor 2, acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2
Replication factor 3, acks=1, min.insync.replicas=2
hld:message-queue.explanation: With acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2 an ack means at least two replicas have the record, so one broker can fail without data loss and writes still succeed with two in sync. Requiring 3 (or using RF 2 with min 2) blocks writes when one broker is down, and acks=1 ignores min.insync.replicas and can lose the data.

hld:message-queue.prompt: Orders are keyed by customerId so each customer's events stay ordered inside one partition. Later the topic grows from 12 to 24 partitions. What is the risk?
options: Existing records are automatically spread over the new partitions and redelivered to consumers
Ordering is unaffected, because Kafka remembers which partition each key was placed on before
Brokers reject keyed writes until the topic has been deleted and recreated
The key-to-partition mapping changes, so new events for a customer can land on another partition
hld:message-queue.explanation: The default partitioner computes a hash of the key modulo the partition count, so changing the count remaps keys. Order within one partition still holds, but a single customer's stream can be split across two partitions around the change. This is why partition counts are planned up front.

hld:message-queue.prompt: A consumer commits its offset first and then processes the record. It crashes halfway through processing. After the restart, what happens to that record?
options: It is processed again, creating a duplicate (at-least-once)
The broker holds it until the consumer confirms completion
It is moved to a dead-letter topic automatically
It is skipped and effectively lost (at-most-once)
hld:message-queue.explanation: The committed offset says the record was handled, so the restarted consumer resumes after it and the work is never done. Committing after processing flips the failure into a possible duplicate, which idempotent consumers can tolerate. Brokers neither track completion of application work nor create dead-letter topics on their own.

hld:message-queue.prompt: One record always makes the consumer throw. Retrying in place blocks its partition, and silently skipping hides the problem. What is the standard handling?
options: Retry a few times, then send it to a dead-letter topic, commit past it and alert
Delete the partition that contains the record and then recreate it empty
Raise max.poll.interval.ms so that the consumer has more time to succeed eventually
Stop the whole consumer group until engineers have fixed the offending record by hand
hld:message-queue.explanation: A dead-letter topic isolates the poison message so the rest of the partition keeps flowing, while keeping the bad record and its error for diagnosis or replay. Stopping the group halts healthy traffic, longer poll intervals do not fix a deterministic failure, and deleting a partition destroys unrelated records.

hld:message-queue.prompt: A consumer's handler takes up to 6 minutes per batch, but the maximum allowed gap between poll calls is 5 minutes. The group keeps rebalancing. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The member misses the poll deadline and is evicted; use smaller batches or a longer interval
The brokers are running out of disk space, so add more brokers to the cluster
The internal offsets topic is corrupt, so it has to be deleted and recreated
There are more consumers than partitions, so remove some of the extra consumers
hld:message-queue.explanation: A consumer that does not call poll within max.poll.interval.ms is considered failed, so the coordinator removes it and triggers a rebalance, and it rejoins and gets removed again. Reducing batch size, speeding up the handler or raising the interval fixes it. Extra consumers simply sit idle without triggering loops.

hld:message-queue.prompt: A topic carries the latest profile record per user id, and a new service must rebuild its in-memory state by reading it from the beginning. Retention by time would drop users who have not changed recently. Which cleanup policy fits?
options: No cleanup at all, so that every record is kept forever
Delete retention based on total topic size only, ignoring the age of the records entirely
Delete retention with a very long time window, such as several years of data
Log compaction, keeping the latest record per key and using tombstones for deletes
hld:message-queue.explanation: Compaction guarantees at least the latest value for each key survives, so a full read rebuilds current state, and tombstones delete keys. Time or size retention eventually removes the only record for quiet keys, and keeping everything forever grows without bound while retaining obsolete versions.

hld:message-queue.prompt: Select all statements that are correct about exactly-once behaviour in Kafka-style systems.
options: Exactly-once also covers any side effects the consumer performs in an external database
Idempotent producers use a producer id and sequence numbers so the broker can drop a retried duplicate batch
Transactions let a consume-process-produce loop atomically write output records and commit its input offsets
With transactions on, consumers no longer need idempotent logic for external systems
hld:message-queue.explanation: Idempotence handles duplicates from producer retries, and transactions make read-process-write within Kafka atomic. A write to an outside database is not part of that transaction, so the consumer still needs idempotency or an outbox. The network cannot give true exactly-once delivery, only effectively-once processing.

hld:message-queue.prompt: Select all reasons why a log-structured broker can sustain very high throughput.
options: Recent data is served from the OS page cache, and sendfile moves bytes to the socket without copying through user space
Every message is individually fsynced to guarantee durability before the next append
Appends are sequential, which disks and SSDs handle at near hardware speed
The broker keeps all messages in a large in-heap cache and avoids disk reads
Producers batch and compress many records so the per-message overhead is amortized
hld:message-queue.explanation: Sequential appends, reliance on the page cache with zero-copy sends, and batching plus compression are the main throughput levers. Kafka does not fsync every message (durability comes from replication), and it deliberately avoids a large heap cache, leaning on the kernel instead.

hld:message-queue.prompt: A consumer group can increase its parallelism beyond the topic's partition count simply by adding more consumers.
options: True
False
hld:message-queue.explanation: Within a group each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so consumers beyond the partition count sit idle. To scale further you must add partitions, which is why partition count caps consumer parallelism and has to be planned.

hld:message-queue.prompt: With acks=all, the leader waits until every replica assigned to the partition has the message, including replicas that have fallen out of the in-sync set.
options: True
False
hld:message-queue.explanation: The leader waits for the members of the in-sync replica set only. Lagging replicas are removed from it, which keeps one slow follower from blocking writes. If the set shrinks below min.insync.replicas, the broker rejects the write rather than risk loss.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: A fleet exposes 60 million active time series, and every series is scraped once every 15 seconds. What sustained ingest rate, in samples per second, must the pipeline handle?
options: About 4 million
About 900 thousand
About 15 million
About 60 million
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Each series yields one sample per scrape, so the rate is 60M / 15 s = 4M samples/s. Quoting 60M confuses the number of series with the sample rate, and 15M multiplies by the interval instead of dividing by it.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Ingest is 5 million samples per second. A raw sample is 16 B (8 B timestamp + 8 B value); with Gorilla-style delta-of-delta and XOR compression assume 1.5 B per sample. About how much storage does one day of compressed data need?
options: About 650 GB
About 69 TB
About 6.9 TB
About 65 GB
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: 5M x 1.5 B = 7.5 MB/s, times 86,400 s is about 648 GB per day. The 6.9 TB figure is what you get without compression (5M x 16 B x 86,400 s), which is the tempting wrong answer; 65 GB drops a factor of ten.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: A developer adds a user_id label (about 2 million distinct values) to a request counter that already carries service and status labels. What is the most likely consequence, and the best remedy?
options: The Kafka topic runs out of partitions; add partitions by series hash
Each sample gets larger on disk; tune compression and extend retention
Series count and memory multiply; drop user_id and keep per-user detail in logs or traces
Queries return wrong values because labels get re-sorted; rewrite the dashboards
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Every unique label combination is a new series, so the series count and head-block and index memory grow multiplicatively, slowing ingestion and queries. Compression and extra partitions do not fix that; unbounded identifiers belong in logs or traces, or behind quotas.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: A team keeps only the average per 5-minute window in its long-term rollups. Why can they not, in general, compute a correct 1-hour average from the twelve stored averages?
options: Rollups discard timestamps, so the twelve windows cannot be located
Windows can contain different numbers of samples, so the plain mean of means is skewed; sum and count fix it
An average is undefined unless min and max are stored next to it
Averages overflow floating-point storage; they should store integers
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: A window with 5 samples and one with 30 must be weighted differently. Storing sum and count lets you add them and divide at query time, which stays correct for any window size. Min and max are kept for spike visibility, not to make averages valid.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Each of 1,000 hosts exports its own latency p99 every minute. How do you get a correct fleet-wide p99 for the service?
options: Average the per-host p99 values, weighted by each host's request count
Take the median of the per-host p99 values
Export histogram bucket counts, sum them across hosts, then estimate the quantile from the merged buckets
Take the maximum of the per-host p99 values and report that as the fleet p99
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Quantiles cannot be combined by averaging or taking a max or median of per-host quantiles; each of those gives a different number from the true p99. Histogram bucket counts are additive, so merging buckets and then computing the quantile is the correct approach.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: The metrics pipeline and its alert evaluator run in the same cluster as the services they watch, and the whole cluster loses power. Which design still gets someone paged?
options: Show a red banner on the dashboards so on-call notices on their next visit
An always-firing heartbeat alert sent to an external service that pages when it stops arriving
Alert on a cluster_up metric evaluated by the existing evaluator
Add another evaluator replica inside the same cluster so one can take over
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: The alerting path must not depend on what it monitors. A dead-man's-switch heartbeat checked by an independent external service turns silence into a page. Anything evaluated inside the failed cluster goes down with it, and a dashboard only helps if someone is looking.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: A nightly batch job runs for about 5 seconds, while the collector scrapes targets every 15 seconds. How should its metrics reach the system?
options: Keep the job process alive for an hour after it finishes so it can be scraped
Have the job push its final values to an intermediary (a push gateway) that the collector scrapes
Lower the global scrape interval to 1 second so the job is always caught
Skip metrics for batch jobs and rely on logs only
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Pull cannot reliably see short-lived jobs, so they push to an intermediary that stays up and is scraped normally. A 1 second global interval multiplies ingest for every target; keeping a process alive just to be scraped is a hack that wastes resources.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: One database host dies and 50 dependent alerts start to fire. Which alert manager features reduce the page storm? Select all that apply.
options: Shortening the 'for' duration so every alert fires sooner
Inhibition rules that suppress dependent alerts while the node-down alert is firing
Running more evaluator replicas and sending each replica's copy as its own notification
Grouping related alerts into a single notification
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Grouping merges related alerts into one message and inhibition mutes symptoms while the root cause is firing. A shorter 'for' makes alerts fire faster, which adds noise, and unduplicated replica copies multiply it; replicated evaluators need deduplication, not separate pages.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Select all statements that are true about placing a Kafka topic between collectors and TSDB writers in a metrics pipeline.
options: It absorbs ingestion spikes so writers can lag briefly without samples being lost
Partitioning by series hash keeps each series' samples ordered on one partition and one writer
It lowers end-to-end latency compared with collectors writing straight to the TSDB
It removes the need for per-tenant series quotas
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: The buffer decouples collectors from storage and absorbs bursts, and keying by series hash preserves per-series order. It adds a hop, so latency goes up rather than down, and it does nothing about cardinality: a flood of new series still lands in the TSDB.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Because the TSDB writes immutable, time-partitioned blocks, retention can be enforced by deleting whole expired blocks rather than deleting rows one by one.
options: True
False
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Each block covers a fixed time range, so expiring old data is a cheap file delete, and queries can also skip blocks outside the requested range. Row-by-row deletes would be expensive in a write-heavy, compressed layout.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: An alert rule has a 'for' duration of 5 minutes, so the rule's expression is only evaluated once every 5 minutes.
options: True
False
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: The rule is still evaluated at the normal evaluation interval (for example every 30 to 60 s). The 'for' duration only requires the condition to stay true across those evaluations for 5 minutes before the alert fires, which filters out blips.

hld:email-service.prompt: An SMTP edge server replies '250 OK' as soon as it holds the DATA in memory, and writes the message to the inbound queue a moment later in the background. What is the flaw?
options: SMTP forbids writing to a queue after the final reply
If the server crashes in between, the sender believes delivery succeeded but the message is gone
The reply to the end of DATA must be 354 rather than 250
The sender will retry immediately and cause a duplicate on every single message
hld:email-service.explanation: Once we say 250, responsibility for the message transfers to us, so it must already be durable. Replying early opens a window where an acknowledged message can vanish. If we cannot persist it, we should answer with a temporary 4xx so the sender keeps it and retries.

hld:email-service.prompt: While delivering outbound mail, a remote server answers one recipient with a 451 temporary error and another with a 550 'mailbox does not exist'. What should the sender workers do?
options: Retry the 550 recipient from another IP and drop the 451 one
Retry both with backoff for several days, since any error may clear
Reschedule the 451 recipient with exponential backoff; stop on the 550 and send a non-delivery report to the sender
Bounce both immediately so the queue does not grow
hld:email-service.explanation: 4xx replies are transient, so the row is rescheduled with increasing delays up to a few days. 5xx is a permanent failure: retrying wastes effort and hurts IP reputation, so we stop and generate a DSN. Dropping a 4xx would lose mail that would have been delivered.

hld:email-service.prompt: Assume 60 million users each receive 30 messages a day. Roughly what is the average inbound rate in messages per second?
options: About 210 thousand
About 2 thousand
About 1.8 million
About 21 thousand
hld:email-service.explanation: 60M x 30 = 1.8 billion messages a day; divided by 86,400 s that is about 21 thousand per second. The 1.8 million figure is the daily total mistaken for a per-second rate; peaks would be a few times higher than this average.

hld:email-service.prompt: Assume 1.8 billion messages a day arrive with an average size of 60 KB including attachments. About how much raw data per day goes to storage, before compression, dedup and replication?
options: About 10.8 TB
About 108 TB
About 1.08 PB
About 18 TB
hld:email-service.explanation: 1.8 x 10^9 x 60 KB = 108 x 10^12 B, about 108 TB per day, or roughly 40 PB per year. That is why bodies and attachments go to a blob store and only about 1 KB of metadata per message stays in the hot store.

hld:email-service.prompt: Mail metadata is partitioned by user_id, and one user's mailbox grows to tens of millions of messages, creating an oversized partition. Which change keeps newest-first folder listing cheap?
options: Re-partition all messages by message_id so load spreads evenly
Move that user's messages into a global table sorted by time
Bucket the partition key as (user_id, month), clustering by folder and time inside each bucket
Partition by received date so each day is one partition
hld:email-service.explanation: Time-bucketing within the user keeps partitions bounded while the newest page of a folder still lives in the latest bucket or two. Partitioning by message_id scatters a listing across the cluster, and partitioning by date creates hot, cross-user partitions.

hld:email-service.prompt: A remote server timed out waiting for our reply after we had already stored its message, so it retries the same message. How do we avoid a duplicate in the recipient's mailbox?
options: Reject any second connection from the same sending IP within an hour
Reply 550 to every retry so senders give up
Accept it and let users delete duplicates themselves
Check the Message-ID, with a content hash, against messages already delivered to that mailbox and drop the repeat
hld:email-service.explanation: Mail transfer is at-least-once, so the receiver makes delivery idempotent by recognising a message it already stored for that user. Blocking by IP rejects legitimate mail, and a 550 would bounce a message that was in fact delivered once.

hld:email-service.prompt: A new reply arrives whose In-Reply-To header matches the Message-ID of a message already stored in the user's mailbox, but the subject line was edited completely. Which thread should it join?
options: The existing thread, because header references take priority over subject matching
The thread with the most similar subject inside a time window
Whichever thread was updated most recently
A new thread, because the subject differs
hld:email-service.explanation: Threading uses In-Reply-To and References first, since they identify the parent explicitly. Normalised subject matching within a time window is only a fallback when no header matches, and recency has nothing to do with conversation membership.

hld:email-service.prompt: Select all statements that correctly describe inbound sender authentication.
